```
scheduler: AddGenericPodGroup can expose a partially populated podGroup to Pop

When a PodGroup (or the last missing CompositePodGroup ancestor) is observed after its pods, `PriorityQueue.AddGenericPodGroup` can make the root group poppable while it holds only one member. The scheduling cycle then runs against a partial group.

Step in `pkg/scheduler/backend/queue`:

1. `podGroupMemberPods.clear` builds the pod list by ranging over a map, so member order is random.
2. `AddGenericPodGroup` calls `addPodGroupMember` once per pod.
3. For the first pod there is no queued root, so `addPodGroupMember` creates the `QueuedPodGroupInfo` with that single pod, calls `moveToActiveQ`, and broadcasts.
4. `Pop` only takes the activeQ lock, not `p.lock`, so the scheduler goroutine can pop the one-member group while `AddGenericPodGroup` is still iterating.
5. Remaining pods then find no queued root, hit `isLastPoppedEntity`, and are parked in `pendingPodGroupPods` until the group is requeued.

This has been reproduced and about 9% of pops under `-race` return a one-member group.

All pods waiting in `incompletePodGroupPods` for a root are added to the `QueuedPodGroupInfo` before the group becomes visible to `Pop`, so the first pod group scheduling cycle sees every member already known to the queue.

You can check the integration flake in #141794 (`TestPodGroupPreemption/Binding first before preemption for gang policy`), where either `high-1` or `high-2` binds first depending on which pod landed in the one-member group.

Its impact is not limited to the test:

- Gang policy: a group popped below `minCount` fails the gang check ("minimum threshold cannot be satisfied"), costing a wasted cycle and a backoff before the full group is retried.
- Basic policy, or gang with `minCount` below group size: the cycle can bind or preempt for a subset, so placement and preemption decisions are made without the full group.

**Proposed fix (from @mm4tt on #141804)**

In `AddGenericPodGroup`, add every pod cleared from `incompletePodGroupPods` to the root info first, then call `moveToActiveQ` and `broadcast` once. The existing-root and last-popped-entity branches of `addPodGroupMember` still need to be honored on that path.

PR #141804 only relaxes the test to match `Bind` without pod names.

Improve pod signing in PodTopologySpread and InterPodAffinity to support Opportunistic Batching with default scheduler configuration

Opportunistic Batching ([KEP-5598](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/5598-opportunistic-batching)) currently accelerates consecutive scheduling cycles of identical pods by:
- **Computing pod signatures on queue insertion**: When a pod enters or is updated in the scheduling queue, the scheduler collects `SignPod` fragments from all enabled plugins to build a pod signature.
- **Reusing node evaluations across identical pods**: For consecutive pods with matching signatures, the scheduler reuses cached node filtering and scoring outcomes and re-evaluates only the node chosen in the previous cycle.
- **Bypassing or flushing when incompatible**: If any plugin marks a pod as unsignable or consecutive pods produce different signatures, batching is skipped and all candidate nodes are evaluated from scratch.

However, under the **default `kube-scheduler` configuration**, Opportunistic Batching (as well as higher-level optimizations built on pod signatures, such as proposed CompositePodGroup Topology-Aware Scheduling in [#142726](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142726)) is effectively disabled for standard workloads due to current pod signing limitations, particularly in `PodTopologySpread` and `InterPodAffinity`:

- **`PodTopologySpread` marks all pods unsignable under default configuration**:
  - By default, `PodTopologySpread` configures system-default soft spread constraints (`ScheduleAnyway` across nodes and zones). Whenever default constraints are present, `PodTopologySpread` currently marks every pod in the cluster as unsignable, even when no default spread selector actually applies to the pod (for example, standalone `Job` or `PodGroup` pods not owned by a `ReplicationController`, `ReplicaSet`, or `StatefulSet` and not matched by any `Service`).
  - Furthermore, workloads such as **JobSet** create a headless `Service` by default (for pod-to-pod DNS discovery) whose selector matches the workload's pods. Because `PodTopologySpread` derives default spread selectors from matching `Service`s in addition to `ReplicationController`, `ReplicaSet`, and `StatefulSet` owners, `JobSet` pods still get the system-default spread constraints applied. Simply allowing pods without `ReplicaSet`/`StatefulSet`/`ReplicationController` owners to be signed is therefore not sufficient on its own to unblock `JobSet` under the default scheduler configuration.
  - Pods with explicit `TopologySpreadConstraints` are similarly unsignable today because Opportunistic Batching assumes strictly node-local side effects.
- **`InterPodAffinity` signs all pod labels and rejects pods with anti-affinity**:
  - Under default settings (`ignorePreferredTermsOfExistingPods: false`), `InterPodAffinity` includes all pod labels in the signature to account for affinity or anti-affinity rules that may exist on scheduled pods in the cluster. Common batch and distributed workloads (such as Indexed `Job`s and `JobSet`) set unique per-pod metadata labels (e.g., `batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index`) that are not referenced by any cluster affinity rules, resulting in a distinct signature per pod and preventing batch reuse.
  - Incoming pods that define their own `PodAntiAffinity` rules (for example, hostname-scoped anti-affinity to place at most one pod per node, or topology-scoped anti-affinity) are also unconditionally unsignable.
- **Queued pod signatures cannot safely embed dynamic cluster state**:
  - Because pod signatures are computed and cached when pods enter the scheduling queue, any signing relaxation that depends on cluster state (such as which label keys are referenced by scheduled pods' affinity rules, or whether a `Service` in the namespace selects the pod) cannot be baked directly into the queued signature without risking stale signatures when cluster state changes (see discussion in [#142726](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142726)).

As a result, under the stock `kube-scheduler` configuration:
- Opportunistic Batching produces no batch hits unless cluster administrators apply custom plugin configuration overrides that alter default scheduling behavior.
- Standard workloads (`Job`, `JobSet`, `ReplicaSet`, `StatefulSet`, `PodGroup`, `CompositePodGroup`) still pay the full per-pod filtering and scoring cost across unaffected nodes.
- Higher-level scheduling optimizations relying on pod signatures (including [#142726](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142726)) cannot benefit common workloads out of the box.

We propose extending Opportunistic Batching ([KEP-5598](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/5598-opportunistic-batching)) and pod signing so that batching works out of the box under the default `kube-scheduler` configuration. Concrete design details and trade-offs should be validated and refined based on a proof-of-concept implementation, focusing on the following high-level areas:

1. **Decouple static pod signatures from dynamic cluster-state batch checks**: Keep the signature cached in the scheduling queue derived strictly from the `Pod` object so queued pods never hold stale signatures, and evaluate cluster-state-dependent batch compatibility at scheduling time as part of the active batch state.
2. **Improve `InterPodAffinity` label handling and `PodAntiAffinity` support**: Restrict label compatibility checks to label keys actually referenced by affinity/anti-affinity rules in the cluster (so unreferenced per-pod metadata labels like `job-completion-index` do not break batching under default settings), and support batching for common `PodAntiAffinity` patterns (such as hostname-scoped and/or topology-scoped anti-affinity).
3. **Support `PodTopologySpread` under default configuration**: Stop unconditionally rejecting all pods when system-default spread constraints are configured: allow batching when no spread selector applies to a pod, and explore supporting batch reuse when default or explicit topology spread constraints are active (including workloads matched by headless `Service`s such as `JobSet`, for example via topology-domain-aware score/feasibility updates).

As a practical implementation trade-off to consider, some of the Opportunistic Batching caching extensions could be scoped to a **single workload scheduling cycle** (such as `PodGroup` or `CompositePodGroup` scheduling, where pods are evaluated against a consistent cluster snapshot) rather than persisted across independent pod-by-pod scheduling cycles. This can simplify cluster-state invalidation while still capturing significant Opportunistic Batching benefits when scheduling larger workloads.

Making Opportunistic Batching functional under the default `kube-scheduler` configuration is essential for practical adoption at scale:
- Most Kubernetes clusters run `kube-scheduler` with default plugin settings; requiring cluster-wide overrides to `PodTopologySpread` and `InterPodAffinity` is impractical in multi-tenant environments.
- Key target workloads for KEP-5598, PodGroup (KEP-4671), and CompositePodGroup (KEP-6012), including Indexed `Job`s and `JobSet` (which combine per-pod index labels with headless `Service`s), currently cannot benefit from batching under default settings.
- Enabling default-config support unlocks the full value of both pod-level Opportunistic Batching and PodGroup/CompositePodGroup scheduling optimizations ([#142726](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142726)) without custom scheduler profiles.
```

```
A `/scale` update that keeps `spec.replicas` unchanged drops the creating manager's ownership of `spec.replicas`; a later server-side apply then changes it without a conflict

A Deployment is created with `kubectl create` (manager `kubectl-create`, operation `Update`) and `spec.replicas: 2`. A server-side apply of `spec.replicas: 5` by another manager is refused with a conflict, as documented. Then `kubectl scale --replicas=2` is run twice, which does not change the value.

- The first scale write splits the `kubectl-create` entry of `managedFields` into two entries with the same manager, operation and apiVersion: one without `time` that owns only `spec.replicas`, and one with the rest of the fields.
- The second scale write removes the entry without `time`. Now no manager owns `spec.replicas`.
- The same server-side apply of `spec.replicas: 5` now succeeds without `--force-conflicts`, and the Deployment scales from 2 to 5.

Each scale write also bumps `resourceVersion` although nothing changed.

The [Server-Side Apply page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/server-side-apply/#field-management) says: "Whenever a field's value does change, ownership moves from its current manager to the manager making the change." and "When trying to apply an object, fields that have a different value and are owned by another manager will result in a conflict." In [Conflicts](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/server-side-apply/#conflicts): "This prevents an applier from unintentionally overwriting the value set by another user." Here the value did not change, but ownership was lost, and the applier overwrote the creator's value with no conflict. The [ObjectMeta reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/common-definitions/object-meta/) says "ManagedFields maps workflow-id and version to the set of fields that are managed by that workflow", but after the first write the same workflow and version appear twice.

Scripts and controllers that run `kubectl scale` (or write `/scale`) with the current value are common, for example an HPA or a CI job that re-asserts the replica count. After two such writes, any applier takes over `spec.replicas` silently.

A `/scale` write that does not change `spec.replicas` keeps ownership as it is: one `kubectl-create` entry that still owns `spec.replicas`, no new `resourceVersion`, and the last apply is refused with the same conflict as the first.

```
kubectl create -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: web}
  template:
[... 22 more lines]
```

Output (v1.37.2; the `spec=` column prints `{}` when the entry owns `spec.replicas`):

```
deployment.apps/web created
error: Apply failed with 1 conflict: conflict with "kubectl-create" using apps/v1: .spec.replicas
Please review the fields above--they currently have other managers. Here
are the ways you can resolve this warning:
[...]
deployment.apps/web scaled
rv=187
kubectl-create/Update/apps/v1 time= spec={}
kubectl-create/Update/apps/v1 time=2026-11-16T12:04:36Z spec=
deployment.apps/web scaled
[... 4 more lines]
```

The same happens with `PUT .../deployments/web/scale` and any field manager for the scale write. It does not happen when the creator used server-side apply (operation `Apply`).

**Potential cause.** The manager identifier of an `Update` entry includes its apiVersion; only `Apply` entries leave it out ([`managedfields.go#L147-L151`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/954517dcb5c79593a5787a3071b925976a64b285/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/internal/managedfields.go#L147-L151)). `ScaleHandler.ToSubresource` keeps the parent identifier (with `apps/v1`) as the map key but gives the entry apiVersion `autoscaling/v1` ([`scalehandler.go#L78-L86`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/954517dcb5c79593a5787a3071b925976a64b285/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/scalehandler.go#L78-L86)). When the scale entries come back to `ToParent` and are decoded again, their identifier contains `autoscaling/v1`, so `scaleFields[manager]` misses for the parent's `Update` entry ([`scalehandler.go#L128-L146`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/954517dcb5c79593a5787a3071b925976a64b285/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/scalehandler.go#L128-L146)). The parent entry loses `spec.replicas` ("steal"), and the scale entry is added back as a second `apps/v1` entry with no time, because `t[manager]` is looked up with the scale identifier ([`scalehandler.go#L149-L160`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/954517dcb5c79593a5787a3071b925976a64b285/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/scalehandler.go#L149-L160)). On the next write the two entries share one identifier, and the one that owns `spec.replicas` is lost.

**Suggested fix.** Match scale entries to parent entries by manager, operation and subresource without the apiVersion (or keep a map from scale identifier to parent identifier in `ToSubresource`), so an unchanged owner is found in `ToParent` and its entry is kept as it is.

Not a regression in recent releases: v1.34.1 behaves the same.
```

```
VolumeBinding Filter cost grows with nodes × CSIStorageCapacity objects

For a pod with an unbound `WaitForFirstConsumer` PVC whose CSI driver sets `storageCapacity: true`, the VolumeBinding Filter calls [`hasEnoughCapacity`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/eb24fe4e932bf95877653f89b4720fbdc8429353/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L976-L1048) for every node. For each node it:

1. lists every CSIStorageCapacity in the cluster with `csiStorageCapacityLister.List(labels.Everything())` ([L1000](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/eb24fe4e932bf95877653f89b4720fbdc8429353/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L1000));
2. for each object in the PVC's StorageClass with enough capacity, calls `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector(capacity.NodeTopology)` until it finds one that matches the node ([L1036-1048](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/eb24fe4e932bf95877653f89b4720fbdc8429353/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L1036-L1048)).

Drivers for node-local storage run external-provisioner with `--node-deployment --enable-capacity`, which publishes one CSIStorageCapacity per node per StorageClass. Filter cost per pod is then:

```
O(nodes that reach VolumeBinding × CSIStorageCapacity objects)
```

The [TODO at L999](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/eb24fe4e932bf95877653f89b4720fbdc8429353/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L999) ("benchmark this and potentially introduce some kind of lookup structure") is still open, and no Go benchmark or scheduler_perf workload exercises this path.

Observed on a production cluster (Kubernetes 1.36.1, about 1,750 nodes, 1,427 of them with local NVMe and one CSIStorageCapacity each, `percentageOfNodesToScore` unset):

- When a batch job frees about 300 NVMe nodes at once, each queued pod with a local ephemeral volume takes **1.3–2.2 s** per scheduling cycle. The scheduler trace shows more than 99% of it in `"Computing predicates done"`, with `evaluatedNodes=1751 feasibleNodes≈290`.
- In one 5-minute episode, 305 such pods used about 192 s of scheduler time. Other pods waited up to about 3 minutes for their first scheduling attempt.
- Pods without PVCs stay under 100 ms with the same number of feasible nodes.
- When few nodes are free, the same pods schedule in about 65 ms, because busy nodes fail `NodeResourcesFit` before reaching VolumeBinding.

The capacity check for one node should not need to list and convert the selector of every CSIStorageCapacity in the cluster, so Filter cost shouldn't grow with the total number of CSIStorageCapacity objects.

Benchmark PR: #144143 (adds `BenchmarkFilter` to `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/volume_binding_test.go`). Run with:

```
go test ./pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/ -run '^$' -bench BenchmarkFilter -benchmem
```

It is modeled on podtopologyspread's `BenchmarkFilter`: PreFilter, then Filter on every node through the framework parallelizer, for a pod with one unbound `WaitForFirstConsumer` PVC and one CSIStorageCapacity per node. Results on an Apple M4 Pro:

| Case | Time per pod | Memory per pod | Allocations per pod |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 nodes, no capacity tracking | 12.5 ms | 7.8 MiB | 89k |
| 1,000 nodes, 1,000 CSIStorageCapacities | 37.7 ms | 243 MiB | 5.6M |
| 5,000 nodes, 5,000 CSIStorageCapacities | 1,213 ms | 6.1 GiB | 137M |

Possible directions, smallest first:

1. **Cache the converted selector per CSIStorageCapacity.** `nodeTopology` is immutable, so a selector stays valid for the object's lifetime. This removes the per-node `LabelSelectorAsSelector` calls but keeps the linear scan. There's precedent in noderesources' `nodeMatchCache` and in `AffinityTerm.Selector`.
2. **Index CSIStorageCapacity by StorageClass and `matchLabels` entry**, for example from the driver's `CSINode` topology keys, with a linear fallback for selectors that use `matchExpressions`. This removes the dependency on the total object count. VolumeBinding already indexes PVs by StorageClass (`storageClassIndex`), and nodevolumelimits indexes VolumeAttachments by node.

I'm happy to work on this.

Indexed Job: possible overlap between `failedIndexes` and `completedIndexes`?

In an edge case with an Indexed Job and `backoffLimitPerIndex`, the same index may end up in both `status.failedIndexes` and `status.completedIndexes`:

1. Indexed Job with `backoffLimitPerIndex` (e.g. `0`) and default pod replacement.
2. A pod for an index is deleted while not `Succeeded` (e.g. autoscaler interruption). That can count the index as failed and write it into `failedIndexes`.
3. The same pod later becomes `Succeeded` (process exits 0), so the index is also added to `completedIndexes`.
4. Because `failedIndexes` is sticky from prior status, the two sets may overlap.

Per the API docs, failed indexes should not overlap completed indexes. If success is the later outcome, the index should be dropped from `failedIndexes` so status updates are not rejected by the overlap validation.

If this is deemed worth remedying: when calculating failed indexes, omit indexes already in the succeeded / completed set (“success wins”), at least for indexes carried from `.status.failedIndexes`.

Requeue pods rejected for DRA node allocatable resources without waking pods that wait for other DRA devices

Follow up item from the discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142768#discussion_r4560561905

With DRANodeAllocatableResources (KEP-5517), the DynamicResources plugin checks in Filter whether the pod's spec plus the node allocatable DRA resources fit the node. NodeResourcesFit runs before it and only sees the spec, so DRA plugin could reject the pod for insufficient cpu, memory, hugepages or ephemeral-storage if the combined footprint (spec + DRA ) does not fit on the node.

A queueing hint cannot tell whether DRA rejected a pod because devices were missing or because node allocatable resources did not fit. And Requeueing is per plugin, to wake these pods when capacity frees up, the DynamicResources plugin would have to register AssignedPod Delete and UpdatePodScaleDown. So every pod DRA rejected would be woken on every pod delete or scale down, including pods waiting for devices, and each wake-up re-runs device allocation which is costly.

Before DRANodeAllocatableResources is enabled by default, pods rejected because their node allocatable resources do not fit should be requeued when capacity frees up (pod delete, pod scale down, node allocatable change), without waking pods that only wait for other DRA devices.

PodGC can force delete a same-named replacement pod because its delete has no UID precondition

`markFailedAndDeletePodWithCondition` in `pkg/controller/podgc/gc_controller.go` force deletes pods by name, with a zero grace period and no UID precondition. The pods come from PodGC's informer cache. For pods that are already in a terminal phase (`Succeeded`/`Failed`), the UID-pinned status patch is skipped, so nothing ties the delete to the pod PodGC actually observed.

The StatefulSet controller deletes a pod in a terminal phase and recreates it under the same name (`pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go`). That allows this sequence:

1. PodGC lists pods and sees the failed `web-0` (terminated-pod threshold exceeded, or its node was deleted).
2. The StatefulSet controller deletes `web-0` and creates a new `web-0`.
3. PodGC sends a name-only, grace period 0 delete for `web-0` and force deletes the new running pod.

This breaks the StatefulSet guarantee of at most one pod per ordinal. The window grows when PodGC has many deletes queued behind its client rate limit, for example in a large cluster over `--terminated-pod-gc-threshold`.

PodGC only deletes the pod it observed. `devicetainteviction` already guards against this race with a UID precondition (`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go`).

The race is timing dependent. A unit test reproduces it: put a terminal pod in PodGC's informer cache, put a same-named pod with a different UID in the apiserver, run `gc()`, and the replacement is deleted.

Proposed fix: add `Preconditions: metav1.NewUIDPreconditions(string(pod.UID))` to the delete options. I have a PR ready.

kubelet retries NodePublishVolume without restaging after a CSI staging mount is lost

During a CephFS incident, nine Pods using the same PVC were stuck in `ContainerCreating`. The expected CephFS mount was missing, while local XFS mounts remained at the staging and old Pod publish paths. CSI repeatedly reported:

```
staging path .../globalmount ... is not a mountpoint
```

kubelet kept retrying `NodePublishVolume` without calling `NodeStageVolume` again. Clearing the incorrect mounts and restarting kubelet restored service.

The incident involved Kubernetes v1.28.11 and Ceph CSI v3.7.2.10. We then separately reproduced the lack of restaging after staging loss in an isolated minikube environment.

Environment: Kubernetes `v1.38.0-beta.0.185+041ecc5eea9c06`, upstream Ceph CSI v3.15.0, Ceph 19.2.7, CephFS kernel mounter and an RWX PVC.

1. Start Pod A using the PVC. Verify successful Stage/Publish and write a test file on CephFS.
2. On the test node, use ordinary `umount` on only that volume's exact staging target. Keep Pod A's publish mount and kubelet running.
3. Create Pod B using the same PVC on the same node.
4. Pod B stays in `ContainerCreating`. During a 64-second observation window, there are **8 failed Publish calls and 0 Stage calls**. Pod A can still read the test file through its existing mount.
5. Keep both Pods and restart kubelet. Stage and Publish are called again, Pod B becomes Ready, and both Pods can read the original file.

This also reproduces with `CSIGlobalMountReconstruction=true`.

Could kubelet work with CSI drivers to reissue `NodeStageVolume` and then retry Publish when the driver explicitly confirms that staging has been lost, without requiring a kubelet restart? The driver would remain responsible for mount identity validation and the actual mount operations.

Could this build on `NodeGetVolumeHealth` from [KEP-1432](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-storage/1432-volume-health-monitor), or would a separate explicit CSI signal be needed?

[KEP-3756](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-storage/3756-volume-reconstruction) and [KEP-6058](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-storage/6058-csi-global-mount-fallback), including merged PR #138454 and the earlier open PR #136771, address reconstruction after a restart. This request concerns staging loss while kubelet remains running.

scheduler: Improve TestPlugin support for multi-pod scheduling scenarios

Improve the scheduler's TestPlugin test infrastructure to support scenarios involving multiple pods, where state from one pod's scheduling cycle affects another.

Ideally, tests could run multiple pods through the relevant scheduling framework phases while keeping the shared plugin state consistent with actual scheduler behavior.

This would be particularly useful for testing DRA pending allocations shared between pods, as discussed in #144080.

While working on #144080, we needed to simulate a scenario where one pod had already reserved a ResourceClaim allocation and another pod reused that pending allocation during its scheduling cycle.

The current tests require manually constructing parts of that shared state, which makes it easy to introduce inconsistencies between the test setup and what actually happens in the scheduling framework.

Better multi-pod support in TestPlugin would make these scenarios easier to reproduce, maintain, and validate.

This is a follow-up to the [review discussion in #144080](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/144080#discussion_r4556375736), as suggested by @nojnhuh. It is not required for that PR or the v1.38 release.

DRA: Pod waits ~5 min for a device released by a deleted Pod that was waiting on BindingConditions [1.37 regression]

When a Pod that is waiting for `BindingConditions` in `PreBind()` is deleted, another Pod that needs the same device stays Pending for about 5 minutes, although the actual device becomes free within seconds.

The cluster has one device, whose `BindingConditions` are never satisfied.
One Pod (`a`) is allocated the device and waits in `PreBind()`.
I deleted `a`, and created another Pod (`b`) that requests the same device right away.

On v1.37.0, the scheduler rejected `b`.
`a`'s `PreBind()` ended 5 s after the deletion and freed the device, but `b` stayed Pending for 313 s:

```
21:14:08 b  FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 cannot allocate all claims.
21:14:13 kube-scheduler: PreBind of a: could not find ResourceClaim "default/a-dev-jrb46"
21:19:21 b  BindingConditionsPending (b is allocated the device)
```

On v1.36.4, `b` is allocated the device at once (0 s).

If a uses a standalone `ResourceClaim` that is not deleted with `a`, `a`'s `PreBind()` holds the device until the claim is deleted (over 2 min in our test), or up to `bindingTimeout`.

`b` is allocated the device within seconds after `a` is deleted, as in v1.36.

```
kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.37.0 --wait 1m

kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceClass
metadata: {name: example}
spec:
  selectors: [{cel: {expression: 'device.driver == "example.com"'}}]
---
# Nobody sets "Ready", so a Pod using dev-0 waits in PreBind.
[... 30 more lines]
```

v1.37.0:

```
21:14:08 FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 cannot allocate all claims.
21:14:13 (scheduler) PreBind of a: could not find ResourceClaim "default/a-dev-jrb46"   <- dev-0 is free
21:19:21 BindingConditionsPending (b got dev-0 after 313 s)
```

v1.36.4: b gets dev-0 at once (0 s).

With a standalone ResourceClaim that outlives Pod a, a's PreBind keeps dev-0 until the claim is deleted (we saw over 2 min), or up to `bindingTimeout`.

b gets dev-0 within seconds after a is deleted, as in v1.36.

Cause:

- Since #139418, the in-flight allocation is released only when `PreBind()` succeeds or in Unreserve ([dynamicresources.go#L1850](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L1850)), so it is held for the whole `BindingConditions` wait
  - v1.36 released it once the claim was in the assume cache ([v1.36.4#L1533](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.4/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L1533))
- After Unreserve, `handleBindingCycleError` requeues with `EventAssignedPodDelete` only ([schedule_one.go#L529](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L529))
- DynamicResources does not register for `EventAssignedPodDelete` ([#L278](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L278)), so `b` stays unschedulable until the 5-minute flush
- `PreBind()` keeps polling a deallocated claim
  - It is never ready, and `isClaimTimeout` skips claims without an allocation ([#L2034](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L2034))

Related:

- #139418
  - keeps the in-flight allocation until PreBind succeeds or Unreserve runs)
- #143463
  - another regression from #139418, device allocated twice after a PreBind failure; does not change the points above
- #135474
  - BindingConditions feedback

scheduler: DRA extended resource scoring uses stale device-match and node-match caches (never invalidated, wrong capacity until restart)

The `NodeResourcesFit` scoring path for DRA-backed extended resources uses two persistent `sync.Map` caches in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/resource_allocation.go`.

Neither cache accounts for changes to all inputs that affect matching results:

| Cache | Cache key | Missing dependency |
|---|---|---|
| `deviceMatchCache` | CEL expression, driver, pool, device name | Device attributes and capacity |
| `nodeMatchCache` | Node name, target node, allNodes, selector | Node labels |

Both caches use `Load`/`Store` without any invalidation or eviction mechanism. Cached results persist for the lifetime of the scheduler process.

This causes two independently reproduced bugs.

A device that previously matched a DeviceClass CEL selector remains cached as matching after its ResourceSlice is republished with attributes that no longer satisfy the selector.

| State | Actual matching GPUs | Scorer reports |
|---|---:|---:|
| H100 + A100 | 1 | 1 |
| H100 + H100 | 2 | 2 |
| H100 + A100 (downgraded) | **1** | **2 (stale)** |
| After scheduler restart | 1 | 1 |

The allocator correctly evaluates updated attributes, while `NodeResourcesFit` continues using the old cached match result.

`deviceMatchCache` only stores successful (`true`) matches. Failed matches return before caching. Therefore, the stale direction is *previously matching → no longer matching*, leading to overcounted capacity.

A ResourceSlice uses `perDeviceNodeSelection`, with one device gated by a NodeSelector.

After adding the required label, the allocator recognizes the device as available, but scoring continues to use a previously cached `false` match.

| State | Actual matching GPUs | Scorer reports |
|---|---:|---:|
| Without matching label | 1 | 1 |
| After adding label | **2** | **1 (stale)** |
| After scheduler restart | 2 | 2 |

Unlike `deviceMatchCache`, `nodeMatchCache` stores both positive and negative results. Node label changes can therefore cause either overcounting or undercounting.

- Incorrect DRA extended resource capacity estimates for `LeastAllocated`, `BalancedAllocation`, and relevant placement-scoring paths.
- Potentially skewed scores and suboptimal node selection.
- Stale results persist across scheduling cycles until kube-scheduler restarts.
- No explicit error or metric indicates that matching results are stale.

**Filtering/allocation correctness is unaffected by these scoring caches.** The issue is that the allocator and scorer can evaluate the same resource state with different matching results during the same scheduling cycle.

Reproduced on Kubernetes v1.36.5. The affected cache implementation was also confirmed on master (`7bd6e5e0c87`, 1.38-dev).

DRA resource scoring should reflect Node labels and ResourceSlice device attributes/capacity available in the current scheduling snapshot.

When these inputs change, previously cached matching results must not remain valid indefinitely.

Possible approaches include:

- Invalidating matching results when dependent objects change.
- Including missing inputs in cache keys.
- Scoping matching-result caches to a scheduling cycle.
- Removing result caching while retaining `celCache`, which caches compiled CEL expressions rather than matching outcomes.
```

```
APF queueSet removes an excess queue while a lingering request still holds seats in it, then panics or corrupts fairness when that request's seats are released

In `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/queueset.go`, a request that has finished its main service but still holds seats during its `AdditionalLatency` (a "lingering" request, e.g. a mutating request whose work estimate reserves seats for its watch fan-out) is removed from its queue's set of executing requests immediately in `finishRequestLocked`, while the release of its seats is deferred to an `EventAfterDuration` callback that fires when the `AdditionalLatency` elapses.

`removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` decides whether to drop an excess queue (one of the queues draining after `DesiredNumQueues` was reduced) using:

```
if len(qs.queues) > qs.qCfg.DesiredNumQueues &&
    r.queue.requestsWaiting.Length() == 0 &&
    r.queue.requestsExecuting.Len() == 0 {
    qs.queues = removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes(qs.queues, r.queue.index)
    ...
}
```

It does not check `r.queue.seatsInUse`. So when a queue Q holds a lingering request `r` (whose seats are still counted in `Q.seatsInUse`) plus another request `s`, and `s` finishes, the guard sees no waiting and no executing requests and removes Q — even though `r` still occupies seats in it. `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes` renumbers only the queues kept in `qs.queues`, so the removed Q keeps a now-stale `index` and `r.queue` still points at it. When `r`'s lingering timer later fires, its deferred `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked(r)` runs `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes(qs.queues, <stale index>)` a second time, on a slice that no longer contains Q:

- if the stale index is at or past the end of the now-shorter slice, `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes` panics with `slice bounds out of range`;
- otherwise it removes a different, live queue, silently corrupting the round-robin index bookkeeping and seat accounting of the remaining queues.

The panic runs in the goroutine spawned by `eventclock.Real.EventAfterDuration`, which has no `recover`, so it crashes the whole kube-apiserver process.

An excess queue should not be removed while a lingering request still holds seats in it. It should then be removed exactly once, by the lingering request's own deferred `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` call after its seats are released (which happens before the deferred call, in `releaseSeatsLocked`), through an index that is still valid.

Unit-level, with the queueset's fake event clock (test in `package queueset`):

1. Build a queuing queueset with `DesiredNumQueues: 3`, `HandSize: 1`, ample concurrency.
2. `StartRequest` two requests with the same hash (they share a queue): `r` with `WorkEstimate{InitialSeats: 1, FinalSeats: 1, AdditionalLatency: time.Second}` (lingering) and `s` ordinary.
3. Reconfigure to `DesiredNumQueues: 1` (the three queues remain and drain by attrition).
4. `r.Finish(...)` — it lingers on one seat for one second. Then `s.Finish(...)` — the queue is removed although `r` still holds seats.
5. Advance the fake clock past the `AdditionalLatency`.

Result on current master (`dbe731cf4b0`): the queue is gone after step 4, and step 5 either panics (when the shared queue is the last one, stale index 2 against a 2-element slice) or removes a wrong queue. I have a regression test that fails at step 4 with "got 2 queues while the lingering request still holds seats, want 3"; with the shared queue mapped to index 2 the old code panics at step 5.

The trigger needs an operator to reduce a PriorityLevelConfiguration's `queuing.queues` (so excess queues are draining by attrition) together with the right concurrent traffic and timing, so the probability is low; but the consequence — an apiserver crash from a no-recover goroutine, or silent fairness corruption — is severe, and the code path is reachable through supported configuration. I did not find a way for an unprivileged user to trigger it on their own, so I am filing this as a regular bug.

Proposed fix: add `&& r.queue.seatsInUse == 0` to the `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` guard. `releaseSeatsLocked` decrements `r.queue.seatsInUse` before its deferred `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked(r)` runs, so the deferred call then sees `seatsInUse == 0` and removes the queue through the still-valid index. Queues without lingering requests are unaffected.

Kubelet doesn't reconcile partial failures configuring pod cgroups

Kubelet creates the pod cgroup directory and configures it in 2 separate steps. Failures during cgroup configuration are only logged, and subsequent SyncPod iterations only check for the existence of the cgroup, so Kubelet never reapplies the configuration.

Full Explanation (AI summary)

When the kubelet sets up a pod's cgroup in [`SyncPod`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/69a8e1ff31556386089beebee70216693c229c10/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2231-L2243), it gates `pcm.EnsureExists` on `!pcm.Exists(pod)`, and [`podContainerManagerImpl.EnsureExists`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/69a8e1ff31556386089beebee70216693c229c10/pkg/kubelet/cm/pod_container_manager_linux.go#L79-L112) likewise returns early if `m.Exists(pod)` is true. `Exists` only checks that the cgroup directory and controllers exist on disk; it does not check whether any resource parameters were applied.

Inside [`cgroupCommon.Create`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/69a8e1ff31556386089beebee70216693c229c10/pkg/kubelet/cm/cgroup_manager_linux.go#L417-L428), cgroup creation happens in two steps:

```
if err := manager.Apply(-1); err != nil {
	return err
}

// it may confuse why we call set after we do apply, but the issue is that runc
// follows a similar pattern.  it's needed to ensure cpu quota is set properly.
if err := manager.Set(libcontainerCgroupConfig.Resources); err != nil {
	utilruntime.HandleError(fmt.Errorf("cgroup manager.Set failed: %w", err))
}

[... 1 more lines]
```

1. `manager.Apply(-1)` creates the cgroup directory (or starts the systemd `.slice` unit via `StartTransientUnit`) with **no** resource limits. As soon as `Apply(-1)` succeeds, `pcm.Exists(pod)` is `true`.
2. `manager.Set(...)` applies the actual cgroup configuration (via a separate D-Bus `SetUnitProperties` call under systemd, plus direct cgroupfs writes). If `manager.Set` fails, the error is logged with `utilruntime.HandleError` and dropped.

This can leave a pod cgroup unconfigured (or partially configured) in two ways:
- **`manager.Set` returns an error** (for example, a transient systemd D-Bus timeout/error on `SetUnitProperties` after `StartTransientUnit` succeeded, or a cgroupfs write failure). `Create` and `EnsureExists` return `nil`, and `SyncPod` starts the pod's containers in the unconfigured cgroup.
- **The kubelet crashes or restarts between `Apply(-1)` and `Set`** (or if `Create` is changed to return the `Set` error). Because the cgroup already exists on disk, subsequent `SyncPod` calls see `pcm.Exists(pod) == true` and skip `EnsureExists` for the rest of the pod's life.

1. **Propagate `manager.Set` errors from `cgroupCommon.Create`:** Return the error from `manager.Set` instead of swallowing it with `utilruntime.HandleError`, so `EnsureExists` fails and `SyncPod` aborts before starting containers.
2. **Track configured pod cgroups in memory:** Maintain an in-memory record of pods whose cgroup configuration has succeeded.
3. **Make `EnsureExists` idempotent via `Update`:** Gate `EnsureExists` on whether the pod cgroup has been configured rather than just whether the directory exists. If the cgroup directory already exists when `EnsureExists` runs, call `cgroupManager.Update` to apply the configuration. On kubelet restart, the in-memory tracking starts empty, so `EnsureExists` re-runs once per pod to ensure the cgroup configuration is correct and rebuild the in-memory state.

kube-proxy nftables: partial syncs do work proportional to the total number of Services

In nftables mode, a partial sync (`fullSync=false`) already sends nftables only what changed, but kube-proxy itself still does work proportional to the total number of Services to work out what that is. I would like the Go side of a partial sync to cost in proportion to the Services that changed.

On master (dd21ea95bc5), every `syncProxyRules` call, partial or full:

- loops over every entry in `svcPortMap`, calls `CategorizeEndpoints` for it, and builds every map and set element so that `ensureElem` can remove it from `leftoverKeys`. `skipServiceUpdate` only skips writing the chain contents.
- lists every chain and every set in the table (`List("chain")`, `List("sets")`) to find stale chains and affinity sets.
- copies every element key of each map and set back into `leftoverKeys` (`resetLeftoverKeys`).
- rebuilds `HealthCheckNodePorts()` and `LocalReadyEndpoints()` from scratch. Both have a TODO about computing them incrementally.

In addition, `EndpointSliceCache.checkoutChanges` walks the tracker of every Service to find the few that have pending slices.

I measured the cost with a benchmark that applies one EndpointSlice change and syncs, with N single-port Services of 3 endpoints each already programmed. It uses `knftables.Fake` with `Run()` turned into a no-op after the initial sync, so the numbers are kube-proxy's own CPU time and nothing else:

| Services | time per sync | allocations per sync | operations in the transaction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1000 | 3.5 ms | 21,622 | 3 |
| 4000 | 22.5 ms | 85,578 | 3 |
| 16000 | 111 ms | 341,343 | 3 |

At 16000 Services kube-proxy spends about 110 ms and 340k allocations to produce a 3-operation transaction. This is per sync and per IP family, and it comes on top of what the netlink `List` calls cost on a real node, which the fake does not model.

We run nftables mode in a cluster with about 17000 Services, where kube-proxy has a CPU limit of 200m, so per-sync CPU in kube-proxy matters to us.

Related issues and PRs:

- #139513 looked at slow incremental syncs, and attributed them to `nft list` (now replaced by netlink in #137536) and to the kernel. The Go-side loop did not come up.
- #139878 avoids the `List` calls on incremental syncs by remembering the chains and affinity sets. That is one part of what is described here.
- #139328 is about cold start. Nothing here helps with that; full syncs would stay as they are.
- #143804 changes how the per-Service rules are laid out. It has a different goal but touches the same code.

The iptables backend also loops over every Service on a partial sync, but there the shared chains such as `KUBE-SERVICES` have to be rewritten as a whole by `iptables-restore`, so I don't see how to do the same thing for it.

I have an implementation for the nftables backend and will open a PR that references this issue. With it the 16000-Service case above takes about 31 µs and 257 allocations per sync.

kubelet stops negotiating HTTP/2 (no ALPN) when ReloadKubeletClientCAFile is enabled (default since 1.36)

Since 1.36, kubelets that have `--client-ca-file` set no longer negotiate ALPN on the serving port (10250). Every client, including the kube-apiserver, falls back to HTTP/1.1.

The cause is in `NewMainKubelet` ([pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L997-L1006) on master, L963-L972 on v1.36.4), which was added in #136762:

```
if utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.ReloadKubeletClientCAFile) {
	klet.clientCAManager = dynamiccertificates.NewDynamicServingCertificateController(kubeDeps.TLSConfig.Clone(), kubeDeps.Auth, nil, nil, nil)
	...
	kubeDeps.TLSConfig.GetConfigForClient = klet.clientCAManager.GetConfigForClient
```

1. `kubeDeps.TLSConfig` has no `NextProtos` at this point. The kubelet relies on `net/http` to fill them in: `ListenAndServeTLS` in `pkg/kubelet/server/server.go` adds `h2` and `http/1.1` to the TLS config that the listener uses.
2. The dynamic controller clones the config **before** that, so its base config has empty `NextProtos`.
3. For every handshake, crypto/tls uses the config returned by `GetConfigForClient` instead of the listener's config. That config is a clone of the controller's base config, so the `NextProtos` that `net/http` added are never used.
4. Result: the server offers no ALPN, and clients that ask for `h2` get HTTP/1.1.

kube-apiserver avoids this in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/secure_serving.go`, where it sets `NextProtos: []string{"h2", "http/1.1"}` explicitly on the base config before attaching `GetConfigForClient`. The kubelet path doesn't do that.

Same behaviour as with the gate off, or as on 1.35: the kubelet negotiates `h2` on 10250, and clients that ask for HTTP/2 get it.

On any 1.36+ node whose kubelet has `--client-ca-file` set (the default for kubeadm, kind and managed offerings):

```
openssl s_client -connect <node-ip>:10250 -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -i alpn
```

- 1.36.4 (gate on by default): `No ALPN negotiated`
- 1.35.7 (gate doesn't exist): `ALPN protocol: h2`

We measured both on AKS (1.36.4 on three clusters, 1.35.7 on one) with the same node image family. We expect `--feature-gates=ReloadKubeletClientCAFile=false` on 1.36 to restore `h2`, but haven't verified this ourselves because AKS doesn't let us set kubelet feature gates.

**Impact.** The apiserver multiplexes kubelet requests (logs, exec, attach, port-forward, `nodes/proxy` scrapes) over HTTP/2. Without it, every streaming request needs its own TCP+TLS connection to the kubelet. This matters most when apiserver→kubelet traffic runs through Konnectivity (AKS, GKE, and others), because every connection becomes a tunnel connection.

What we measured, with the same workload pattern (log tailing via `pods/log` plus kubelet/cAdvisor scrapes via `nodes/proxy`):

| | kubelet ALPN | tunnel connections | streams |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.35 cluster | `h2` | ~213 | ~6.4k (multiplexed) |
| 1.36 cluster | none | ~1 per stream | ~1 per connection |

On the 1.36 clusters, the extra connection churn coincided with admission webhook calls through the same tunnel timing out (`TLS handshake error from <konnectivity-agent IP>: i/o timeout` in the webhook server). Moving log collection and scrapes out of the tunnel brought connection counts down from ~455 to ~90 and stopped those timeouts. We can't prove causation inside the managed tunnel, so take this as context for the severity, not as part of the bug.

**Suggested fix.** Set `NextProtos` on `kubeDeps.TLSConfig` before cloning it, mirroring kube-apiserver:

```
kubeDeps.TLSConfig.NextProtos = []string{"h2", "http/1.1"}
```

An alternative is to build the dynamic controller from the config after `net/http` has prepared it. Either fix would be worth backporting to 1.36 and 1.37, since the gate is Beta and on by default in both, and managed providers typically don't expose kubelet feature gates as a workaround.

AKS managed; containerd. Not relevant.

PodReadyToStartContainers condition should include sandbox creation error details

When pod sandbox creation fails (e.g., due to a CNI ADD error), the failure detail is only available in `FailedCreatePodSandBox` events on the pod. The `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition — which was specifically designed to surface sandbox readiness — does not include the error from the failed sandbox creation attempt.

After #135300, the condition's `Message` field reports *what state* the sandbox is in (e.g., "no pod sandbox exists", "pod sandbox has no IP address"), but not *why* it got into that state. The actual CNI error (e.g., "failed to set up sandbox network: unable to allocate IP from exhausted range 10.244.0.0/24") is only emitted as an event and then lost from the pod object.

This forces any automation that monitors pod status — operators managing pods on behalf of higher-level objects, CI pipelines waiting for pods to come up, GitOps controllers — to either scrape events (fragile, high-churn, subject to rotation) or sit blind while the pod remains stuck in `ContainerCreating` with no actionable information in its status.

When sandbox creation fails, the `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition message should include the error from the failed attempt — for example:

```
Type:    PodReadyToStartContainers
Status:  False
Reason:  PodSandboxNotReady
Message: "no pod sandbox exists: failed to set up sandbox network: plugin my-cni failed: unable to allocate IP from exhausted range 10.244.0.0/24"
```

This would allow consumers to read the failure reason directly from `pod.status.conditions` without scraping events.

1. Set up a cluster where a CNI plugin will fail — e.g., exhaust the pod CIDR range, misconfigure a bridge name, or use a CNI config that references a missing resource
2. Create a pod
3. Observe that the pod is stuck in `ContainerCreating`
4. Check `kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml` — the `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition says `"no pod sandbox exists"` with no mention of the CNI error
5. The actual error is only visible in `kubectl describe pod <name>` under Events as `FailedCreatePodSandBox`

The sandbox creation error is already available in the kubelet's `SyncPod()` path (where the `FailedCreatePodSandBox` event is emitted), but it is not persisted anywhere that `GeneratePodReadyToStartContainersCondition()` can read. Bridging this gap would require storing the error from the `createPodSandbox` failure so the condition generator can append it to the message.

Related:
- #135299 / #135300 — added static diagnostic messages to `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition
- KEP-3085 — introduced the `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition
```

```
Pod with an ephemeral local volume preempted during PreBind stays pinned to the node

Since #135502 (v1.36), the scheduler preempts a victim in `PreBind` in memory. It cancels the binding cycle and puts the pod back in the queue. It does not delete the pod.

For a pod with an unbound `WaitForFirstConsumer` PVC, VolumeBinding `PreBind` already made API writes _before_ the cancel. It set the `volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node` annotation on the PVC. The cancel does not revert this write, because `Unreserve` only reverts the assume cache. The external provisioner completes, and the PVC is bound to a PV with node affinity to that node.

The victim is back in the queue, but its volume pins it to the node where it was just preempted. The preemptor now uses that room, so the victim does not fit there. It also cannot go to another node. It stays Pending until enough room frees on that node.

Before v1.36, the victim was deleted. Its ephemeral PVC was garbage collected. Its controller created a replacement pod, and the scheduler was free to place it on any node.

The impact is highest for **generic ephemeral volumes on node-local storage**:

- With node-local storage, the PV has node affinity to one node, so the victim is pinned to that node. With zonal storage, the victim can still go to other nodes in the zone.
- With a generic ephemeral volume, the delete before v1.36 also removed the PVC. A persistent PVC survived the delete in v1.35 too, so v1.36 changes little for it.

I observed this with kube-scheduler v1.36.5, a generic ephemeral volume, and a CSI driver that provisions node-local volumes. Scheduler logs and events (pod and node names replaced):

```
13:07:06.118  pod-a      Reserve.VolumeBinding "AssumePodVolumes" node=node-1
13:07:06.135  pod-a      PreBind.VolumeBinding "Updating claims objects to trigger volume provisioning"
13:07:06.252  ds-pod     "Unable to schedule pod; no fit; waiting" err="0/170 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient memory, 169 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]."
13:07:06.252  ds-pod     PostFilter.DefaultPreemption "Pod is a potential preemption victim on node" pod=pod-a node=node-1
13:07:06.253  pod-a      PreBind.VolumeBinding "Failed to bind volumes for pod" err="binding volumes: context canceled"
13:07:06.253  pod-a      "Error scheduling pod; retrying" err="running PreBind plugin \"VolumeBinding\": preempted by DefaultPreemption"
13:07:06.273  pod-a      Event Preempted: "Preempted by pod <ds-pod-uid> on node node-1 (in kube-scheduler memory)."
13:07:09.334  pod-a-pvc  Event ProvisioningSucceeded (PV with node affinity to node-1)
13:07:12.464  pod-a      Event FailedScheduling: "... 1 node(s) didn't match PersistentVolume's node affinity ..."
```

`pod-a` stayed Pending for 13.5 hours. The scheduler placed it on `node-1` only after another pod left that node.

One of these:

- If the PreBind of the victim already made API writes that cannot be reverted, the victim is deleted, as before v1.36.
- The PreBind writes are reverted, so the victim is not pinned to the node.

I did not build a minimal reproduction yet. The conditions are:

1. A StorageClass with `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` and a CSI driver that provisions node-local volumes (PVs with node affinity to one node). Provisioning takes a few seconds (about 3 seconds in my case).
2. A low-priority pod A with a generic ephemeral volume. Its requests fill most of a node.
3. A higher-priority pod arrives while pod A waits in VolumeBinding PreBind. This pod can only run on that node, and it does not fit next to pod A. In my case, this was a DaemonSet pod on a new node.

With v1.36.5, pod A is preempted in memory, its PVC is bound to the node, and pod A stays Pending. In v1.35, the scheduler code deletes pod A instead (see the code paths below), and its replacement can schedule on another node.

Code paths in v1.36.5
<comment>

- A victim in PreBind is cancelled with `CancelPod`, without an API delete: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad950d1cc78b0183c476bd4d3f1934c104229727/pkg/scheduler/framework/preemption/executor.go#L115-L121
- The pod enters the PreBind map before `RunPreBindPlugins`, and it stays cancellable until `MarkPrebound` after PreBind: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad950d1cc78b0183c476bd4d3f1934c104229727/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L457-L470
- `bindAPIUpdate` says `There is no API rollback if the actual binding fails`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad950d1cc78b0183c476bd4d3f1934c104229727/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L545
- `Unreserve` calls `RevertAssumedPodVolumes`, which reverts only the assume cache: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad950d1cc78b0183c476bd4d3f1934c104229727/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/volume_binding.go#L604-L614
- In v1.35.9, only pods waiting on Permit are rejected in memory. Other victims are deleted: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/329000efd0b26bd78155e51e4df449130f0fca00/pkg/scheduler/framework/preemption/preemption.go#L180-L205

</comment>

This concern came up before the merge, in a comment that asks to revert the actions taken during PreBind: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132332#issuecomment-2979447368. I also commented on the PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135502#pullrequestreview-5838397880

Possible fixes:

1. Do not cancel a victim in memory after VolumeBinding PreBind updated its claims. Fall back to the API delete. For example, VolumeBinding can record in the cycle state that `bindAPIUpdate` ran, or PreBindPreFlight can report that the PreBind is not cancellable.
2. Revert the PreBind writes in `Unreserve`, for example remove the selected-node annotation. This races with the external provisioner, which can already be creating the volume.

Related:

- #140082: the preemptor side of the same feature.
- #125491: another problem caused by the PreBind window. A pod waiting in PreBind for its volume has no node name yet, so the Cluster Autoscaler removed the node.

Pods rejected with "CSI driver is not installed on the node" are not requeued when the driver registers without a volume limit

With `preventPodSchedulingIfMissing: true` on a CSIDriver (`VolumeLimitScaling`, on by default in 1.37), NodeVolumeLimits rejects a Pod that uses a volume of that driver with `<driver> CSI driver is not installed on the node` while the driver isn't registered on the node. When the driver then registers, the Pod isn't retried. It stays Pending until the scheduler flushes unschedulable Pods after `podMaxInUnschedulablePodsDuration` (5 minutes). We saw Pods scheduled 4m16s to 4m56s after the driver appeared in the node's CSINode.

[`isSchedulableAfterCSINodeUpdated`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/csi.go#L197-L236) returns `Queue` only when a driver's `allocatable.count` increases. A driver that registers without a volume limit (`max_volumes_per_node` = 0 in NodeGetInfo, so `allocatable` is nil) has an old limit of 0 and a new limit of 0, so the hint returns `QueueSkip`. The hint was added with KEP-4876 (#130007), before KEP-5030 added the "not installed" rejection (#135012, #137343), and wasn't updated for it. Drivers that report a limit don't hit this, because registering raises their count from 0.

The Pod is retried as soon as the driver is added to the node's CSINode.

1. On Kubernetes 1.37, use a CSI driver whose node plugin registers without a volume limit, and set `preventPodSchedulingIfMissing: true` on its CSIDriver. Keep its node plugin off one node, for example with a nodeSelector on its DaemonSet.
2. Create a Pod with a PVC of that driver, pinned to that node. It's Pending with `<driver> CSI driver is not installed on the node`.
3. Let the node plugin run on that node. The driver appears in the node's CSINode within seconds.
4. The Pod stays Pending for up to 5 minutes before it's scheduled.

- Suggested fix: in `isSchedulableAfterCSINodeUpdated`, also return `Queue` when a driver in the new CSINode is missing from the old one. The unit tests (`TestCSILimitsAfterCSINodeUpdatedQHint`) only cover limit raised, decreased and unchanged.
- Workaround: a node taint that the driver removes after it registers. The Node update requeues the Pod through TaintToleration.
- The same delay happens on nodes added by Cluster Autoscaler 1.37.0. The code is the same on master.

Scheduler cache loses a successfully-bound pod after a failed bind response, violating required podAntiAffinity

A Deployment with 2 replicas and a *required* podAntiAffinity
(`labelSelector: k8s-app=example`, `topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname`) ended up with both
replicas on the same node. The affinity configuration is correct, and another feasible node
existed at that moment.

Timeline (UTC, from kube-scheduler and kube-apiserver logs on the same control-plane node):

| time | event |
|---|---|
| T+0 | etcd, kube-apiserver and kube-scheduler restart on all control-plane nodes (scheduler restartCount=56, apiserver/etcd=1; etcd logs `became leader at term N`) |
| T+0 | Deployment rollout creates `pod-a` and `pod-b`; the replicaset controller deletes the two old replicas, which stay Terminating |
| T+0 | scheduler: `0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector, 2 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules` — the terminating old pods are still in the scheduler cache |
| T+21s | scheduler binds `pod-a` to `node-2`: `Plugin Failed ... Post ".../pods/pod-a/binding": unexpected EOF`, then `Failed to bind pod` |
| T+21s | `pod-a` actually gets `spec.nodeName=node-2` and `PodScheduled=True` — the same second |
| T+21s | scheduler logs a burst of `Unexpected EOF during watch stream event decoding`, then `dial tcp ...: connect: connection refused` for lease renewal — the apiserver was restarting |
| T+28s | the old pod on `node-2` leaves the scheduler cache; scheduler binds `pod-b` to `node-2`: `Successfully bound pod to node pod=pod-b node=node-2 evaluatedNodes=3 feasibleNodes=1` |
| T+28s | both replicas are on `node-2` |

Evidence that `pod-a` was really bound while the scheduler believed the bind failed:

- `pod-a.status.conditions[type=PodScheduled].lastTransitionTime` equals the timestamp of the
  `unexpected EOF` bind error (same second), and `spec.nodeName` is set.
- kubelet started `pod-a` normally.
- The apiserver audit log contains no `/pods/pod-a/binding` entry (it falls in the window where the
  apiserver was restarting), while `pod-b`'s binding entry is present.

Because `pod-a` never entered the scheduler cache, `InterPodAffinity` saw `node-2` as empty and
`pod-b` passed the required anti-affinity check. Required anti-affinity is
`IgnoredDuringExecution`, so nothing re-validates the already-bound `pod-a` and the conflict
persists indefinitely.

Either of:

1. The scheduler should treat an indeterminate bind result (transport error / EOF) as
   "possibly bound" and reconcile with the apiserver before forgetting the pod, or
2. the assigned-pod add event should reliably restore the pod into the scheduler cache, so that a
   required podAntiAffinity cannot be violated by a lost bind response.

Not deterministic. It requires the apiserver/etcd to become unavailable during the bind call of one
of two replicas that have a required hostname-scoped podAntiAffinity, while the remaining nodes are
excluded by node affinity (so there is exactly one feasible node). Related reports triggered the
same window with etcd I/O pressure (#100140), scheduler certificate reload (#109367) and scheduler
restart (#126499).

cluster/log-dump: detect_node_failures queries deprecated GCE activity logs, so host errors are never reported

`detect_node_failures` in `cluster/log-dump/log-dump.sh` looks for host errors and automatic restarts in the legacy Compute Engine activity log:

```
gcloud logging read --order=asc \
  --format='table(timestamp,jsonPayload.resource.name,jsonPayload.event_subtype)' \
  --project "${PROJECT}" \
  "resource.type=\"gce_instance\"
   logName=\"projects/${PROJECT}/logs/compute.googleapis.com%2Factivity_log\"
   (jsonPayload.event_subtype=\"compute.instances.hostError\" OR jsonPayload.event_subtype=\"compute.instances.automaticRestart\")
   jsonPayload.resource.name:\"${group}\"
   timestamp >= \"${creation_timestamp}\""
```

Compute Engine activity logs are deprecated (https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/logging/migrating-from-activity-logs-to-audit-logs) and were replaced by Cloud Audit Logs. Host events are now written to the `cloudaudit.googleapis.com/system_event` audit log with `protoPayload.methodName` set to values such as `compute.instances.hostError` and `compute.instances.automaticRestart`, and the instance name is in `protoPayload.resourceName`.

Because the deprecated log name no longer receives these entries, the query returns nothing and the log dump prints an empty `Failures for <group> (if any):` section even when an instance hit a host error or automatic restart. That makes `kubetest.Up` flakes harder to triage, because the dump looks like no infrastructure event occurred.

The same query is duplicated in `kubernetes/test-infra` at `logexporter/cluster/log-dump.sh`.

`detect_node_failures` should read the system event audit log and report host errors and automatic restarts. If the query itself fails, it should say so rather than printing an empty table.

On a GCE project with a recent host event for an instance in a managed instance group:

```
# Current query: returns no entries.
gcloud logging read --project "${PROJECT}" --limit 5 \
  "resource.type=\"gce_instance\"
   logName=\"projects/${PROJECT}/logs/compute.googleapis.com%2Factivity_log\"
   (jsonPayload.event_subtype=\"compute.instances.hostError\" OR jsonPayload.event_subtype=\"compute.instances.automaticRestart\")"

# System event audit log: returns the same events.

```
Some kube-scheduler histograms stay classic because ApplyFeatureGates() runs after SecureServing and Auth are initialized

Similar to #142379 (which tracks `kube-apiserver`), when running `kube-scheduler` with `--feature-gates=NativeHistograms=true`, histograms registered during early config initialization stay classic-only instead of exposing native histogram buckets:

- `workqueue_queue_duration_seconds` / `workqueue_work_duration_seconds`
- `rest_client_request_duration_seconds`
- `apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds`

Meanwhile, scheduler histograms registered later in the same process (such as `scheduler_scheduling_attempt_duration_seconds` and `scheduler_framework_extension_point_duration_seconds`) are exposed as native histograms.

`HistogramOpts.toPromHistogramOpts()` reads `internalmetrics.NativeHistogramsEnabled()` when `Create()` runs at metric registration time. Although #138914 deferred `workqueue` and `restclient` metric registration from `init()` to first runtime construction, and `x509.NewDynamic()` registers `apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds` lazily when authentication options are applied, `kube-scheduler` calls `metricsfeatures.ApplyFeatureGates()` **after** those constructors have already run.

In `Options.ApplyTo()` (`cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/options.go`, lines 226–284), `metricsfeatures.ApplyFeatureGates(utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate)` is called on **line 270**, after:
- **Line 259**: `o.SecureServing.ApplyTo(&c.SecureServing)`, which constructs dynamic serving cert workqueues (`workqueue_*`) before line 270.
- **Lines 263–268**: `o.Authentication.ApplyTo(...)` and `o.Authorization.ApplyTo(...)`, which construct a REST client (`rest_client_*`) and x509 authenticator (`apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds`) before line 270.

`metricsfeatures.ApplyFeatureGates(...)` should be called immediately after `o.ComponentGlobalsRegistry.SetFallback()` in `Options.ApplyTo()` (before `SecureServing.ApplyTo`, `Authentication.ApplyTo`, and `Authorization.ApplyTo`), matching `kubelet` and `kube-proxy`.

In `KubeControllerManagerOptions.Config()` (`cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/options/options.go`, lines 511–559), `metricsfeatures.ApplyFeatureGates(utilfeature.DefaultMutableFeatureGate)` is called on **line 549**, after:
```

```
kubelet reports a resource request of zero for pods using pod-level resources, so eviction picks them ahead of higher priority pods

The kubelet computes a resource request of **zero** for a pod that uses
pod-level resources, for every resource that is not set at the pod level.

`GetResourceRequestQuantity` in `pkg/api/v1/resource/helpers.go` asks
`PodRequests` to skip container-level resources whenever any pod-level resource
is set:

```
hasPodLevelResources := utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.PodLevelResources) && resourcehelper.IsPodLevelResourcesSet(pod)

if rQuantity, ok := resourcehelper.PodRequests(pod, resourcehelper.PodResourcesOptions{SkipContainerLevelResources: hasPodLevelResources, ExcludeOverhead: true})[resourceName]; ok {
```

`PodRequests` then never aggregates the containers, and only pod-level values
are written back — and `applyPodLevelResources` copies only the resources that
pod-level resources support, which is cpu, memory and hugepages. Everything
else comes back absent, so the quantity stays zero.

Two ways to hit it:

- **`ephemeral-storage` is never a pod-level resource**, so *any* pod that uses
  pod-level resources reports a zero ephemeral-storage request, no matter what
  its containers request.
- Pod-level resources may be **partial**. A pod that sets only cpu at pod level
  reports zero for memory, and vice versa.

This matters because node-pressure eviction ranks on "does this pod exceed its
requests" **before** it ranks on priority
(`pkg/kubelet/eviction/helpers.go:820-834`):

```
orderedBy(exceedMemoryRequests(stats), priority, memory(stats)).Sort(pods)
orderedBy(exceedDiskRequests(...),     priority, disk(...)).Sort(pods)
```

With a request of zero, any usage at all "exceeds", so the pod is put in the
evict-first bucket ahead of higher-priority pods that are within their requests.
The last comparator then sorts by `usage - request`, which for a zero request is
the pod's entire usage, so it also sorts worst inside that bucket.

`pkg/kubelet/preemption/preemption.go` uses the same helper through
`GetResourceRequest` (lines 216, 231, 281-282), so when the kubelet preempts
pods to admit a critical pod it believes evicting such a pod frees none of the
resource, and evicts more pods than it needs to.

A resource that is not set at pod level should be the sum of the container
requests, exactly as it is for a pod that does not use pod-level resources at
all. Pod-level resources are meant to *override* the container aggregate per
resource, which `applyPodLevelResources` already does; skipping the aggregate
discards the resources it does not override.

Two containers, each requesting `cpu: 500m`, `memory: 1Gi`,
`ephemeral-storage: 1Gi`, so the pod requests cpu=1, memory=2Gi,
ephemeral-storage=2Gi. Calling `GetResourceRequestQuantity` with
`PodLevelResources` enabled gives:

| `spec.resources.requests` | cpu | memory | ephemeral-storage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *(unset — control)* | 1 | 2Gi | 2Gi |
| `cpu: 2` | 2 | **0** | **0** |
| `cpu: 2, memory: 4Gi` | 2 | 4Gi | **0** |
| `memory: 4Gi` | **0** | 4Gi | **0** |

The eviction consequence reproduces as a unit test in
`pkg/kubelet/eviction`: two pods both within their 200Mi memory request and both
using 150Mi, one at priority 100 that sets `cpu` at pod level and one at
priority 1 that does not. `rankMemoryPressure` picks the **priority 100** pod
first:

```
--- FAIL: TestRankMemoryPressureWithPodLevelResources
    Expected pod: low-priority, but got: high-priority-pod-level
```

**These pods are accepted by the API.** Running `ValidatePodSpec` with
`PodLevelResourcesEnabled: true` over all three shapes — pod-level cpu only with
container memory and ephemeral-storage, pod-level memory only with container
cpu, and pod-level cpu+memory with container ephemeral-storage — accepts every
one. Partial pod-level resources are legal, and `ephemeral-storage` can only
ever be requested by containers.

There is a second, smaller defect in the same statement: the feature gate is
only consulted to decide the skip. `SkipPodLevelResources` is never set and
defaults to false, so the pod-level values are applied **even when
`PodLevelResources` is disabled** — so a cluster that turns the gate off after
pods already carry `spec.resources` still has those values drive eviction
ranking.

`pkg/api/v1/resource/helpers.go` is the only place in the tree that sets
`SkipContainerLevelResources`, and no existing test asserts the zero values.

Device Plugin NUMA hints ignore pending device requests from admitted pods with pod-level resources

KevinTMtz pointed out this NUMA accounting problem during review of my PR #143494. I subsequently reproduced and verified the behavior; I did not originally identify it.

- [KevinTMtz's original report](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143494#issuecomment-6647302884)
- [My follow-up reproduction and A/B test results](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143494#issuecomment-6651100852)

With `PodLevelResourceManagers=true`, pod-scoped Topology Manager, and Pods using pod-level CPU/memory resources, consecutive Pod admissions can select the same NUMA affinity without accounting for the first Pod's pending Device Plugin allocation.

For example, a Device Plugin advertises one healthy device on NUMA node 0 and three on NUMA node 1, with `PreStartRequired=false`. Two Pods each request one device at container level. Both Pods are admitted before either application container starts:

1. Pod 1 is admitted with preferred affinity to NUMA node 0.
2. Pod 2 is also admitted with preferred affinity to NUMA node 0.
3. Pod 1 starts and receives the only device on NUMA node 0.
4. Pod 2 starts and receives a device on NUMA node 1, outside its stored admission affinity.

Both device allocations succeed, but Pod 2's actual device placement differs from its admission-time topology decision.

A subsequent deterministic unit-level reproduction against unchanged master at `dbe731cf4b0` exercised the real Topology Manager pod scope, policy merging, Device Manager hint generation, and device allocation code, with mocked device topology and plugin RPCs:

| Policy | Pod-level CPU/memory | Admission affinities for Pod 1 / Pod 2 | Actual device NUMA nodes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `best-effort` | Yes | 0 / 0 | 0 / 1 |
| `restricted` | Yes | 0 / 0 | 0 / 1 |
| `single-numa-node` | Yes | 0 / 0 | 0 / 1 |
| All three policies above | No, control case | 0 / 1 | 0 / 1 |

Device Manager was the only hint provider in that test. It establishes admission-affinity versus device-allocation divergence, not physical CPU/memory/device misalignment on real hardware.

Later Pod admissions should account for Device Plugin resources needed by already admitted Pods, even if their containers have not started yet.

In this example, Pod 2 should not select NUMA node 0 based on the assumption that its only device remains available for both Pods. Admission decisions and subsequent device allocation should remain consistent with the configured topology policy.

`best-effort` does not guarantee strict alignment. The concern is the accounting gap between admission and container startup, including the observed affinity divergence under `restricted` and `single-numa-node`.

This does not prescribe moving the Device Plugin `Allocate` RPC into admission. Admission-time reservation/accounting with allocation at container startup is a candidate for investigation, rather than an established fix.
   ```
