kube-scheduler panics in VolumeBinding Score when a CSIStorageCapacity has maximumVolumeSize but no capacity

kube-scheduler panics with a nil pointer dereference in `VolumeBinding.Score` when the CSIStorageCapacity object that matched a node sets `maximumVolumeSize` but not `capacity`.

Both fields are optional in the API. In Filter, `capacitySufficient` in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go` checks the request against `volumeLimit()`, which prefers `MaximumVolumeSize`, so the node passes and the object is stored as `NodeCapacity` for the dynamic provision. Score in `volume_binding.go` then reads `provision.NodeCapacity.Capacity.Value()` without a nil check.

Score runs in `Parallelizer().Until`, whose workers use `HandleCrashWithContext`, so the panic exits the scheduler process. It happens again on every scheduling attempt for the pod after the restart.

The scheduler does not crash. Score skips a CSIStorageCapacity without `capacity`, because there is no free capacity to score, the same way it already skips a provision whose CSIDriver does not set `storageCapacity`.

With `StorageCapacityScoring` enabled (beta and on by default since v1.37):

1. A CSIDriver with `storageCapacity: true` and a StorageClass with `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` for it.
2. A CSIStorageCapacity for that StorageClass with `maximumVolumeSize: 100Gi`, no `capacity`, and a `nodeTopology` that matches at least two nodes.
3. A pod with a PVC of that StorageClass that requests less than `maximumVolumeSize`.

I reproduced it with a `TestVolumeBinding` case on master. The "storage capacity score" case with only `maximumVolumeSize` set panics at `volume_binding.go:516`. Not tried on a running cluster.

external-provisioner always sets `capacity`, so the standard CSI sidecar does not create such an object. It takes a hand-written object or another capacity controller. The API allows it, and validation requires neither field.

The `Capacity.Value()` call came with storage capacity scoring in #128184 (KEP-4049), behind the alpha gate since v1.33. The gate is on by default since v1.37.

Writing CSIStorageCapacity objects needs RBAC that is normally given only to CSI drivers, so I filed this as a normal bug.

I have a fix with a unit test and will open a PR shortly.

Env file parser uses the first definition of a duplicated key, KEP-3721 says the last one wins

When an env file defines the same variable more than once, a `fileKeyRef` to that variable gets the first value. `ParseEnv` in `pkg/kubelet/util/env/env_util.go` returns as soon as it finds the key.

KEP-3721 says the opposite under "Duplicate Names": "If an environment variable is defined multiple times in the file, the last occurrence takes precedence and overrides any previous values." The kubelet already resolves a duplicated name in a container's `env` list the same way, the last entry wins. Bash also gives the last value when it sources the file.

Because the parser stops at the first match, it also never reads the rest of the file. A syntax error after that line is not reported, although the same error before it fails the container with "couldn't parse env file".

The last definition of the key is used, as the KEP specifies.

Write this env file from an init container and reference `KEY1` with `fileKeyRef`:

KEY1='first'
KEY1='second'

The container gets `KEY1=first`. `bash -c 'source ./file; echo $KEY1'` prints `second`. I checked this with a unit test for `ParseEnv` on master.

`EnvFiles` goes GA in v1.38 with `LockToDefault`, so this is the last release where the behavior can change to match the KEP before GA.

I have a fix with unit tests and will open a PR shortly.

CronJob v2 controller syncCronJob discards Status.Active and LastScheduleTime updates due to pointer re-assignment

In the CronJob v2 controller (`pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go`), when `reconcileCronJob` calls `syncCronJob(ctx, cronJobCopy, jobsToBeReconciled)`, `cronJobCopy` is passed by value as a pointer.

Inside `syncCronJob` (lines 462-468), if an unfinished active job is found in the API server that was missing from the local lister, `syncCronJob` rebinds the parameter variable:
```
if inActiveList(cjCopy, j.ObjectMeta.UID) {
    cronJob = cjCopy
    continue
}
```

Because Go is strictly pass-by-value, assigning `cronJob = cjCopy` reassigns the local parameter inside `syncCronJob`. It does **not** update `cronJobCopy` in the caller (`reconcileCronJob`).

Consequently:
1. All subsequent status updates performed in `syncCronJob`—including appending the newly created job to `cronJob.Status.Active` (line 691) and setting `cronJob.Status.LastScheduleTime` (line 692)—are applied exclusively to `cjCopy`.
2. When `syncCronJob` returns `updateStatusAfterSync = true`, `reconcileCronJob` invokes:
   ```
   jm.cronJobControl.UpdateStatus(ctx, cronJobCopy)
   ```
3. `reconcileCronJob` updates the API server with `cronJobCopy`, which **does not contain** the newly created job in `Status.Active` or the updated `LastScheduleTime`!
4. Furthermore, because `cronJobCopy` has an outdated `ResourceVersion` (since `cjCopy` had the newer version), the call triggers an immediate `409 Conflict` error (`Unable to update status for cronjob`). If it succeeds on retry, it overwrites the status and erases the active job reference.
5. On the subsequent sync loop, the controller discovers the unrecorded job and emits a false-positive warning:
   `Saw a job that the controller did not create or forgot: ...`

### What did you expect to happen?

When `syncCronJob` creates a new job or updates status fields, those updates must be reflected in the object passed to `UpdateStatus`, preserving `Status.Active`, `LastScheduleTime`, and the matching `ResourceVersion`.
[... 20 more lines]
```go
cronJobCopy := cronJob.DeepCopy()
...
requeueAfter, updateStatusAfterSync, syncErr := jm.syncCronJob(ctx, cronJobCopy, jobsToBeReconciled)
...
if updateStatusAfterCleanup || updateStatusAfterSync {
    if _, err := jm.cronJobControl.UpdateStatus(ctx, cronJobCopy); err != nil { // <--- Updates cronJobCopy!
```

Callee in `syncCronJob` (lines 449-469):
```go
func (jm *ControllerV2) syncCronJob(
	ctx context.Context,
	cronJob *batchv1.CronJob,
	jobs []*batchv1.Job) (*time.Duration, bool, error) {
...
		if inActiveList(cjCopy, j.ObjectMeta.UID) {
			cronJob = cjCopy // <--- BUG: Only rebinds local parameter!
			continue
		}
```
And then lines 691-693:
```go
	cronJob.Status.Active = append(cronJob.Status.Active, *jobRef)
	cronJob.Status.LastScheduleTime = &metav1.Time{Time: *scheduledTime}
	updateStatus = true
```
Because `cronJob` was rebound to `cjCopy`, `cronJobCopy` in `reconcileCronJob` is never modified.

### Proposed Fix

Have `syncCronJob` return the mutated `*batchv1.CronJob` (or copy the dereferenced struct `*cronJob = *cjCopy`):

```diff
-func (jm *ControllerV2) syncCronJob(
+func (jm *ControllerV2) syncCronJob(
 	ctx context.Context,
 	cronJob *batchv1.CronJob,
-	jobs []*batchv1.Job) (*time.Duration, bool, error) {
+	jobs []*batchv1.Job) (*batchv1.CronJob, *time.Duration, bool, error) {
```
Or simply update the underlying struct in place:
```diff
 			if inActiveList(cjCopy, j.ObjectMeta.UID) {
- cronJob = cjCopy
+ *cronJob = *cjCopy
 				continue
 			}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a subtle Go pointer-aliasing pitfall that affects CronJob status accuracy and job deduplication during transient informer cache latency.

DaemonSet and Job controllers leak expectations on NamespaceTerminatingCause, stalling reconciliation for 5 minutes

When a `DaemonSet` or `Job` attempts to create pods in a namespace that is currently terminating (e.g. during namespace deletion, eviction, or cluster cleanup), the API server rejects pod creation with a `403 Forbidden` carrying `v1.NamespaceTerminatingCause`.

In both `DaemonSetsController` (`pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go:1099-1110`) and `JobController` (`pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go:1934-1949`), the pod creation goroutines intercept `NamespaceTerminatingCause` and exit early via `return` without decrementing the controller expectations (`CreationObserved`).

Because `CreationObserved` is never called and the pod was never created (meaning the Pod Informer will never emit an `Add` event):
1. The expectation counter for the controller key is permanently left with `adds > 0`.
2. `expectations.SatisfiedExpectations()` returns `false` on every subsequent sync loop.
3. The controller refuses to reconcile the `DaemonSet` or `Job` until the full `ExpectationsTimeout` (5 minutes) expires.
4. During this 5-minute stall, the controller cannot perform status updates, handle pod deletions, or execute cleanup logic for that resource.
5. In addition, `errCh` is not populated, causing the slow-start batching loop to ignore the failure and fail to call `LowerExpectations` for unattempted pods.

When pod creation fails with `NamespaceTerminatingCause`, the controller should decrement the expected creations (`expectations.CreationObserved(logger, key)`) or lower expectations immediately, so the controller does not get locked out of reconciling the resource for 5 minutes.

1. Create a namespace: `kubectl create ns test-terminating`
2. Create a DaemonSet or Job in that namespace:
   ```
   apiVersion: apps/v1
   kind: DaemonSet
   metadata:
     name: test-ds
     namespace: test-terminating
   spec:
     selector:
       matchLabels:
         app: test
     template:
[... 22 more lines]
```go

    ds, metav1.NewControllerRef(ds, controllerKind))

if err != nil {
    if apierrors.HasStatusCause(err, v1.NamespaceTerminatingCause) {
        // If the namespace is being torn down, we can safely ignore
        // this error since all subsequent creations will fail.
        return // <--- BUG: exits without calling CreationObserved!
    }
}
if err != nil {
    logger.V(2).Info("Failed creation, decrementing expectations for daemon set", "daemonset", klog.KObj(ds))
    dsc.expectations.CreationObserved(logger, dsKey)
    errCh <- err
    utilruntime.HandleError(err)
}
```

Prior to the batch loop, `dsc.expectations.SetExpectations(logger, dsKey, createDiff, deleteDiff)` registered `createDiff` expected creations. Exiting at `return` skips `dsc.expectations.CreationObserved(logger, dsKey)`.

The exact same bug is present in `pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go:1933-1949`:

    atomic.AddInt32(&creationsFailed, 1)

Server-side apply: mixed numeric comparison loses scalar intent or bypasses conflicts

Server-side Apply can treat two different, representable numeric magnitudes as equal. A second manager can either acquire a claim without getting its asserted value, or change the first manager's value without force or a conflict. Adding an unrelated field selects between those outcomes. Force also fails to transfer the old claim on the rounded numeric change; a forced exact-integer control correctly transfers it.

This reproduces through real CRD HTTP requests, etcd and GET, with an optional `type: number` field. No required rule, default, CEL, webhook, conversion or schema change is involved.

On separate fresh resources, manager A first applies exact int64 `9223372036854775807`. Manager B then applies without force:

| B's intent | Actual persisted result |
| --- | --- |
| `amount: 9223372036854775808` | Accepted, but the old int64 remains. B acquires the `amount` claim anyway. |
| The same number plus `note: changed` | Accepted; the new binary64 magnitude `2^63` is stored. A and B both retain `amount` ownership. |
| Exact int64 `9223372036854775806` plus the note | Correctly rejected with a conflict. GET confirms unchanged data, claims and resourceVersion. |
| The rounded `2^63` change plus the note, with force | Accepted with the new magnitude, but A and B both retain the numeric claim. |
| Exact int64 `9223372036854775806` plus the note, with force | Accepted; B owns amount and A no longer does. |

A non-forced change to another manager's numeric value should conflict. A successful assertion should not silently discard a different representable scalar while granting its claim. The result of the numeric assertion should not depend on whether B also adds an unrelated string field. With force, the claim on a changed numeric magnitude should transfer to B.

metav1.ParseToLabelSelector silently drops conflicting equality requirements on the same key

`metav1.ParseToLabelSelector("tier=db,tier=web")` returns `MatchLabels{tier: web}` with no error. Converted back via `LabelSelectorAsSelector`, that selector matches `{tier: web}`.

`labels.Parse("tier=db,tier=web")` keeps both requirements, so the selector is a contradiction and matches nothing.

The conversion therefore silently widens what the selector selects for. Reversing the input order (`tier=web,tier=db`) keeps `tier=db` instead — the survivor is whichever equality comes last.

Why: `ParseToLabelSelector` (pkg/apis/meta/v1/helpers.go in apimachinery) routes Equals/DoubleEquals requirements into the `MatchLabels` map with a plain assignment, so a second conflicting equality for the same key overwrites the first. The function already returns errors for other unrepresentable inputs ("equals operator must have exactly one value"), and its doc comment says it "should be kept in sync with the parser in pkg/labels/selector.go" — it just never checks for a conflicting duplicate.

Verified non-issues: duplicate equalities with the same value, and equality combined with `in`/`notin`/exists requirements on the same key, all convert faithfully. Only conflicting Equals/DoubleEquals pairs collide.

Verified on apimachinery v0.37.2 and on the master snapshot module version v0.36.0-alpha.2.0.20261031004447-b26d01364f13. Found via property-based differential testing against `labels.Parse`.

Either reject a conflicting duplicate equality with an error (matching how the function already treats unrepresentable input), or preserve the semantics losslessly — e.g. route the subsequent equality for an already-mapped key into `MatchExpressions` as an `In` requirement.

During Pod admission in kubelet, `devicemanager.Allocate()` assigns physical device IDs to a container, updates the in-memory device allocation state, and persists it to disk in `/var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/kubelet_internal_checkpoint`.

If container admission subsequently fails (e.g., due to an image pull secret error, admission webhook rejection, pre-start hook failure, or runtime sandbox creation error) and kubelet is restarted or terminated before `RemovePod()` cleanup completes, the checkpoint file retains the allocation entry for the failed container.

Investigate goroutine panic handling issues

PR #143845 added HandleCrash calls to the concurrent watch decoder’s goroutines. During review, we found that adding a panic handler alone was not enough. If a worker recovers from a panic without publishing a result, its caller can wait indefinitely. Recovery must also ensure that failures are reported and callers can finish.

We then used an AI agent to inspect the code for similar goroutine panic handling issues. Its findings are copied below.

These findings are based on code inspection, without runtime reproductions. We would like human reviewers to inspect each reported issue, determine whether it is a real bug, and provide fixes and tests where appropriate.

---

Follow-up scan for similar goroutine panic-handling issues, at `09faea49b4fc`.

I used an AST scan of 10,135 non-`_test.go` Go files, excluding `vendor`, covering 782 goroutine starts, and inspected the candidate recovery/completion paths and their callers. These are existing follow-ups outside this PR's four added defers. No tests or runtime reproductions were executed; the findings below are based on code inspection.

**1. [P2] The streaming package's `HandleCrash()` does not recover a panic.**

[`k8s.io/streaming/pkg/runtime.HandleCrash`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/streaming/pkg/runtime/runtime.go#L43) delegates to `HandleCrashWithLogger()`, which calls `recover()` indirectly. The [Go specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Handling_panics) requires `recover()` to be called directly by the deferred function. Consequently, `defer runtime.HandleCrash()` does not provide the documented recovery or panic logging.

There is a concrete caller in the [CRI streaming terminal-resize goroutine](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/cri-streaming/pkg/streaming/remotecommand/httpstream.go#L409). A panic there can still terminate the process. The helper needs to call `recover()` directly, or the caller should directly defer the contextual/logger variant.

**2. [P2] WebSocket `Reader.Copy()` can wait forever when serving exits before its handler runs.**

[`Reader.Copy()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/streaming/pkg/httpstream/wsstream/stream.go#L117) starts `websocket.Server.ServeHTTP` and waits on `<-r.err`. Only [`r.handle()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/streaming/pkg/httpstream/wsstream/stream.go#L135) arranges to close that channel.

A rejected handshake returns from `ServeHTTP` without invoking `r.handle()`. A recovered panic during setup/hijacking has the same missing-completion problem. In either case, the goroutine exits without publishing or closing `r.err`, leaving `Copy()` blocked. This path uses the streaming package's own `HandleCrashWithContext`, which recovers without consulting apimachinery's flag.

The [API-server streaming response writer](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/responsewriters/writers.go#L70) calls this method. Completion/error propagation needs to cover every `ServeHTTP` exit. The neighboring [`Conn.Open()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/streaming/pkg/httpstream/wsstream/conn.go#L225) already handles server exit before initialization explicitly.

Each of the following requires both an explicitly enabled non-crashing mode and a panic in the indicated operation. With the default `ReallyCrash = true`, these handlers re-panic. I found no production assignment to `false` in this repository; the in-tree assignments are in tests.

**3. [P2] Exec/attach error-stream recovery leaves a missing result.**

In [`watchErrorStream()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/remotecommand/errorstream.go#L39), a panic in `io.ReadAll(errorStream)` or `d.decode(message)` exits the goroutine after recovery without sending to `errorChan` or closing it: the close is an ordinary statement after the sends.

The protocol stream then waits on `<-errorChan`, for example in [v4](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/remotecommand/v4.go#L80). With a non-cancelled context, the operation can remain stuck. The panic path needs to deliver a failure result and complete the channel; merely closing it would allow a receiver to mistake the zero `error` value for success.

**4. [P2] ListPager recovery can report an incomplete list as successful.**

In [`eachListChunkBuffered()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/pager/pager.go#L221), `err` starts as nil and is assigned only when `p.eachListChunk(...)` returns. If `PageFn` panics, that assignment never completes. The cleanup defer closes `chunkC` and sends the still-nil `err` to `bgResultC`.

After recovery, `EachListItem()` / `EachListItemWithAlloc()` can therefore return nil after delivering only a prefix of the list. The recovery path needs to populate an error before completion is published.

**5. [P2] Discovery recovery can silently omit a group/version.**

In [`fetchGroupVersionResources()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/discovery/discovery_client.go#L1072), a panic while fetching resources skips both the resource insertion and the `failedGroups` insertion. The worker still completes its wait-group entry, and the [caller can return incomplete results with a nil error](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/discovery/discovery_client.go#L946).

The [memory discovery cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L392) has the same missing-result pattern and subsequently sets `cacheValid = true`. Recovered failures should be recorded in the corresponding group/version error entry.

**6. [P2] DeleteCollection can finish before its panic error is published.**

In the [DeleteCollection worker](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go#L1409), `wg.Done()` is deferred after `HandleCrashWithContext`, so it runs first. On the last worker's panic, `workersExited` can close before the panic handler sends its error to `errs`.

The [result check](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go#L1518) is non-blocking and can therefore take the `default` branch and report success before that error arrives. Panic reporting needs to finish before `wg.Done()` releases the waiter.

These resemble the original motivation for this PR, but absence of `HandleCrash` alone is not proof of a defect or a reason to add recovery without examining completion semantics:

- [etcd watch processing](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L593): scheduler, collector, and per-event transform goroutines have no panic handlers. This is especially close to the client-go concurrent decoder. The collector does select on context cancellation while awaiting a per-event result, unlike the unconditional receive discussed in this PR.
- [client-go port forwarding](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go#L488): error-stream reader and the two copy goroutines.
- [`watch.Filter`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/filter.go#L62): the goroutine invokes the supplied filter callback without recovery.
- [`AggregateGoroutines`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/errors/errors.go#L238): each goroutine invokes a supplied callback and sends its result without recovery. Adding recovery alone would leave its fixed-count receiver waiting for a missing result.

For comparison, [`watch.Broadcaster.loop()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09faea49b4fc3904dc5d963263098942d61b6879/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/mux.go#L265) explicitly documents that it deliberately does not catch panics, so I excluded it from the missing-handler candidates.

Panic handling should work as intended.

List with `limit` and `resourceVersion` (no `resourceVersionMatch`) is served at the latest revision, not the exact one, when the field selector names one object

A list request with `limit=<n>` and `resourceVersion=<rv>`, `rv` not 0, and no
`resourceVersionMatch` is served at `<rv>`, except when the field selector names a single object:

- `GET /api/v1/namespaces/<ns>/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.name=<name>&...`
- `GET /api/v1/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.namespace=<ns>,metadata.name=<name>&...`

These two return the object as it is now and set the list's `metadata.resourceVersion` to the
current revision. The same request without the name selector, or with `resourceVersionMatch=Exact`
added, returns the object as of `<rv>`.

A field selector should not change the revision a list is read at. `metadata.name=x` in namespace
`demo2` selects the same object as the request without it, and that request is read at `<rv>`.

All four requests below return `x` with `k: old` and list `resourceVersion` equal to `$RV1`, as the
first and the last do.

```
kubectl create namespace demo2
RV1=$(kubectl -n demo2 create configmap x --from-literal=k=old -o jsonpath='{.metadata.resourceVersion}')
kubectl -n demo2 patch configmap x --type=merge -p '{"data":{"k":"new"}}'
echo "RV1=$RV1"
show() { echo "$1"; kubectl get --raw "$1" | jq -c '{listRV: .metadata.resourceVersion, items: [.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, k: .data.k, rv: .metadata.resourceVersion}]}'; }
show "/api/v1/namespaces/demo2/configmaps?limit=1&resourceVersion=$RV1"
show "/api/v1/namespaces/demo2/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.name=x&limit=1&resourceVersion=$RV1"
show "/api/v1/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.namespace=demo2,metadata.name=x&limit=1&resourceVersion=$RV1"
show "/api/v1/namespaces/demo2/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.name=x&limit=1&resourceVersion=$RV1&resourceVersionMatch=Exact"
```

Output (v1.37.2):

```
namespace/demo2 created
configmap/x patched
RV1=87
/api/v1/namespaces/demo2/configmaps?limit=1&resourceVersion=87
{"listRV":"87","items":[{"name":"x","k":"old","rv":"87"}]}
/api/v1/namespaces/demo2/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.name=x&limit=1&resourceVersion=87
{"listRV":"88","items":[{"name":"x","k":"new","rv":"88"}]}
/api/v1/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.namespace=demo2,metadata.name=x&limit=1&resourceVersion=87
{"listRV":"88","items":[{"name":"x","k":"new","rv":"88"}]}
/api/v1/namespaces/demo2/configmaps?fieldSelector=metadata.name=x&limit=1&resourceVersion=87&resourceVersionMatch=Exact
[... 1 more lines]
```

The second and third requests return revision 88 and `k: new`.

**Potential cause.** When the field selector names one object, `Store.ListPredicate` lists that
object's key with `Recursive = false`
([`store.go#L532-L539`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7fcbfc43c69ef8c0dc2e491c293d60fcef058429/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go#L532-L539)).
The cacher sends every non-recursive exact read to etcd
([`cacher.go#L1459-L1463`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7fcbfc43c69ef8c0dc2e491c293d60fcef058429/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L1459-L1463)),
after the delegator has classified the request as a "Legacy exact match" without looking at
recursion
([`delegator/interface.go#L50-L53`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7fcbfc43c69ef8c0dc2e491c293d60fcef058429/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator/interface.go#L50-L53)).
In etcd, `ValidateListOptions` pins the revision for the legacy case only when `opts.Recursive` is
true
([`interfaces.go#L416-L419`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7fcbfc43c69ef8c0dc2e491c293d60fcef058429/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/interfaces.go#L416-L419)),
so the read happens at the current revision. Explicit `resourceVersionMatch=Exact` pins the revision
for non-recursive reads too, which is why the last request is right.

Before the merge of `GetToList` into `GetList` (#106948), `GetToList` honoured only explicit
`Exact`, so this looks long-standing rather than new.

**Suggested fix.** Drop `opts.Recursive` from the legacy case in `ValidateListOptions`, so a
non-recursive list with `limit` and a non-zero `resourceVersion` is read at that revision (and gets
`410 Gone` when it is compacted), as a recursive one is.

Not a regression in recent releases: v1.34.1 behaves the same.

SSA /status acquires ownership of additional root fields reset by the CRD status strategy

Server-side Apply on a CRD's `/status` subresource can acquire ownership of an unchanged, non-status root field that the status strategy restores from the old object. The original main-endpoint manager's subsequent change then conflicts with that status ownership.

This requires a valid root property outside `spec` and `status`, such as `settings`. It uses one API version, no conversion webhook, no admission webhook, no default, and no force. The same literal manager name is used on both endpoints; its main and status identities are correctly distinct.

A `/status` Apply should not acquire ownership of fields that its REST strategy resets. A subsequent main-endpoint Apply by the original owner should be able to change its `settings.desired` value without force.

The conventional `spec` control behaves as expected: `/status` neither changes nor claims spec, and the main endpoint neither changes nor claims status.

Create this structural CRD:

```
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: examples.status-ownership.example.test
spec:
  group: status-ownership.example.test
  scope: Cluster
  names:
    plural: examples
    singular: example
[... 21 more lines]
```

Wait for the CRD to be Established, then apply on the main endpoint:

```
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=A -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: status-ownership.example.test/v1
kind: Example
metadata:
  name: demo
settings:
  desired: one
YAML
```

Next apply on `/status`, including the unchanged non-status value:

```
kubectl apply --server-side --subresource=status --field-manager=A -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: status-ownership.example.test/v1
kind: Example
metadata:
  name: demo
settings:
  desired: one
status:
  observed: ready
YAML
```

Stored settings remains `one`, and status becomes `ready`. Inspect ownership:

```
kubectl get examples.status-ownership.example.test demo -o yaml --show-managed-fields
```

There are two Apply entries for manager `A`. The main entry owns `settings.desired`; the entry with `subresource: status` unexpectedly owns both leaves:

```
manager: A
operation: Apply
subresource: status
fieldsV1:
  f:settings:
    f:desired: {}
  f:status:
    f:observed: {}
```

Now try the original manager's main-endpoint change:

```
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=A -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: status-ownership.example.test/v1
kind: Example
metadata:
  name: demo
settings:
  desired: two
YAML
```

It fails with an ownership conflict against the status manager for `.settings.desired`. The status endpoint could never persist a change to that field. Data, managedFields and resourceVersion remain unchanged after rejection.

`customresource.statusStrategy.GetResetFields` excludes only `metadata` and `spec`. `PrepareForUpdate` restores every old non-status field while retaining the newly computed managedFields. Therefore an additional root field passes the ownership filter despite being restored by the REST strategy.

Reproduced with a real local apiextensions-apiserver and etcd, using the production implementation from Kubernetes `aedfaadf0d9a70d819ad681bec674f50ccb42975` and its vendored SMD v6.4.2. The test additions change no production behavior. This is a source-checkout reproduction on macOS arm64; released-version coverage has not been established.

The draft formalization PR #143805 adds `TestSSAStatusResetOwnership`, including conventional spec/status controls, exact leaf ownership, same-name subresource identities, the HTTP conflict and unchanged stored state. `ResetCounterexamples.broad_status_reset_contract_is_false` supplies a kernel-checked reachable witness; its normalized primitive boundary is explicit, independently of the HTTP test.

Test: https://github.com/sttts/kubernetes/blob/5820c63b04564744eed64a5f5c8cd4a6e979c915/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/test/integration/ssa_formal_test.go

Proof and boundaries: https://github.com/sttts/kubernetes/blob/5820c63b04564744eed64a5f5c8cd4a6e979c915/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/formal/SSA/ResetCounterexamples.lean

Related historical issue: #75564 addressed ownership of REST-wiped fields. This reproduction shows the remaining additional-root case after the normal spec/status filtering was introduced; the conventional prefix controls pass.

kubelet: node /etc/hosts entries shadow hostAliases in hostNetwork Pods

For `hostNetwork: true` Pods, kubelet writes the node's `/etc/hosts` first and appends `spec.hostAliases` after it ([`nodeHostsFileContent`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/671745e4ffcf3ee0110f6446ef3b5f032db2c51c/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L549-L550)):

```
buffer.Write(hostsFileContent)                         // node /etc/hosts
buffer.Write(hostsEntriesFromHostAliases(hostAliases)) // spec.hostAliases
```

When the node already has an entry for the same hostname, lookups return the node's address first. For example, Go's resolver returns `[<node IP> <hostAliases IP>]`. Clients connect to the first address, so the Pod's `hostAliases` entry is effectively ignored.

We hit this with a kube-apiserver static Pod that pins the OIDC issuer hostname via `hostAliases`. A stale manual entry for the same name in the node's `/etc/hosts` won, and OIDC authentication broke while the Pod spec looked correct.

`hostAliases` entries take precedence over the node's `/etc/hosts`. The setting closest to the workload should win:

- The [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/network/customize-hosts-file-for-pods/) describe `hostAliases` as a "Pod-level override of hostname resolution".
- Docker with `--network host --add-host` drops the host's file ["so that it's possible to override a hostname that's in the host's hosts file"](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/402d0a16f131d93ee89f1b06cb5fc8c98e766dfc/daemon/libnetwork/sandbox_dns_unix.go#L124-L136) ([discussion](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/48823#issuecomment-2461777129)).
- Podman writes `--add-host` entries [before the base file](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/container-libs/blob/52ffcc0844765694b6bfbb492ceac121ef24512e/common/libnetwork/etchosts/hosts.go#L51-L53), which is the host's `/etc/hosts` by default.

Cluster-wide list with `fieldSelector=metadata.namespace=<ns>` and `limit` repeats objects or ends early on the continued page

A cluster-wide list (`GET /api/v1/configmaps`, `kubectl get -A`) with
`fieldSelector=metadata.namespace=<ns>` and `limit` returns wrong pages after the first one:

- If the object names sort before `<ns>`, the second page starts again at the beginning of the
  namespace, so objects are returned twice.
- If the object names sort after `<ns>`, the second page is empty and has no `continue` token, so
  the client stops and the remaining objects are never returned.

The unpaged list (`--chunk-size=0`) is correct. The same request against the namespaced path
(`/api/v1/namespaces/<ns>/configmaps?limit=...`) is correct.

The [API reference for the `limit` parameter](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/config-map-v1/)
(List All Namespaces) says: "If limit is specified and the continue field is empty, clients may
assume that no more results are available." and "The server guarantees that the objects returned
when using continue will be identical to issuing a single list call without a limit".
[API concepts, Retrieving large results sets in chunks](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#retrieving-large-results-sets-in-chunks):
"By continuing until the server returns an empty `continue` value, you can retrieve the entire
collection."

`kubectl get -A --field-selector metadata.namespace=<ns>` uses `--chunk-size=500` by default, so it
shows wrong output once the namespace holds more than 500 objects of the kind. Any client that pages
a cluster-wide list with this selector (client-go's pager, for example) is affected the same way.

The pages together hold each object of the namespace exactly once, as the unpaged list does:
`a1 a2 a3` in `demo` and `x1 x2 x3` in `other` below.

```
kubectl create namespace demo
kubectl create namespace other
for n in a1 a2 a3; do kubectl -n demo create configmap $n --from-literal=k=v; done
for n in x1 x2 x3; do kubectl -n other create configmap $n --from-literal=k=v; done

kubectl get configmaps -A --field-selector metadata.namespace=demo --chunk-size=0
kubectl get configmaps -A --field-selector metadata.namespace=demo --chunk-size=2
kubectl get configmaps -A --field-selector metadata.namespace=other --chunk-size=0
kubectl get configmaps -A --field-selector metadata.namespace=other --chunk-size=2
```

Pod QoS class should be derived from effective pod resources

Without pod-level resources, a pod is Guaranteed only if *every* container, including init containers, has requests == limits. But the kubelet sizes the pod cgroup from the effective pod resources (`PodRequests`/`PodLimits`), where init containers are combined with `max`. So a pod can be Burstable even though its effective requests equal its limits and its cgroup is configured exactly like a Guaranteed pod's.

With pod-level resources, QoS comes from `spec.resources`, so writing the same values at the pod level makes the pod Guaranteed.

A non-restartable init container has requests < limits, and those limits fit within the regular containers' resources. Pods without init containers aren't affected.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: qos-example
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: init
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["true"]
    resources:
[... 8 more lines]
```

`qos-example-plr` is the same pod with `spec.resources` set to requests = limits = `{cpu: "2", memory: 2Gi}`. On v1.37:

| Pod | QoS | cgroup parent | `cpu.max` | `cpu.weight` | `memory.max` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `qos-example` | Burstable | `kubepods-burstable` | `200000 100000` | 79 | 2Gi |
| `qos-example-plr` | Guaranteed | `kubepods` | `200000 100000` | 79 | 2Gi |

The pod cgroups are identical; only the QoS class differs.

Compute QoS from the effective pod cpu/memory resources for all pods (excluding overhead). This is already the rule for pods with pod-level resources. Only pods shaped like the example would change, from Burstable to Guaranteed.

- **Compatibility:** `status.qosClass` is set at creation, so only new pods change. The class still drives the cgroup parent, OOM score adjustment, eviction order, and anything matching on `qosClass`.
- **CPU/memory managers:** a Burstable init container in a Guaranteed pod must not get exclusive resources. Pod-level resources already handle this with `IsContainerEquivalentQOSGuaranteed`; the same check would apply here.
- **Version skew:** an older kubelet could receive such a pod marked Guaranteed and give the init container exclusive CPUs or memory.

WAS: preferred topology level for PodGroups

A second, optional topology level on a `PodGroup` that the scheduler treats as a preference. The group must stay inside the required domain (for example a rack). Inside that domain the scheduler should try to pack the group into a smaller domain (for example a host) when it fits, and fall back to the rack when it does not. Both levels are evaluated in one scheduling decision.

This is listed in KEP-5732 as future work ("Prioritized Placement Scheduling" and "Optional/Preferred Scheduling Constraints", [Future Extensions](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/92eb8a18eb831a21b610dd86053ecab7a663ec46/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#future-extensions).

`TopologyConstraint` has one field, `key`, and the list is capped at one entry [v1beta1 types.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L844-L856). Every constraint is hard.

I am not an expert with the scheduler code, but from my research it seems that the scheduler builds one candidate `Placement` per distinct value of the key ([topology_placement.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cbfc0564b409b82c6ec0cf76e2d15860dd13b31b/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/topologyaware/topology_placement.go#L60-L100)), simulates the whole group in each one, keeps the placements where at least `minCount` pods fit, and commits the one with the best `PlacementScore` ([schedule_one_podgroup.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cbfc0564b409b82c6ec0cf76e2d15860dd13b31b/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go#L997-L1129)). Nested groups resolve top down with KEP-6012 multi-level TAS (#140638): a parent fixes a zone, children pick racks inside it. If no domain fits, the group is unschedulable.

Lease watches cannot keep up with high Lease write rates

On large clusters with high Lease write rates, Lease watchers cannot keep up with the watch stream and get force-closed and reconnected every few seconds, even when using Protobuf. Because Leases have no watch-cache index, their watch channel buffer is capped at 100 events. Under high write throughput, that buffer overflows on every reconnect while the apiserver flushes missed events from the watch cache before draining live incoming writes.

In kube-controller-manager, node health checks still work despite the broken Lease watch because each short-lived watch advances the reflector's resource version within the 40s grace period without re-listing. When the watch lags past 40s, the circuit breaker from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138698 falls back to a live Lease GET and pauses node evictions until the cache catches up. However, this leaves the node controller blind to real node failures while the circuit breaker is open, and it also sends a live Lease GET every 5s for every node that is already marked Unknown.

References:
- [Watch channel buffer cap](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache_history.go#L188-L212)
- [Catch-up event delivery before draining live input](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cache_watcher.go#L450-L532)
- [Node controller lease circuit breaker and live GET check](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller.go#L964-L991)

SSA loses an explicitly empty associative list; required/CEL validation rejects every retry

Server-Side Apply loses an explicitly supplied empty associative list when the same manager releases its previously owned list items.

With no presence constraint, the first request for `endpoints: []` removes the field; an identical second request creates the empty list. With OpenAPI `required: [endpoints]` or CEL `has(self.endpoints)`, the first result is invalid, so every identical retry is rejected and the populated list remains.

This requires only one manager, no defaults, and no mutating webhooks. Creating a new object with the same empty list succeeds under either validation policy.

If manager A is the only owner of the old items and applies a valid `endpoints: []`, the request should empty the list while preserving its explicitly requested presence on the first Apply.

The initial populated object and the requested empty object are both valid under the schema below.

Create this CRD. The root list field is required; its elements have only the key field as a required child.

```
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: ssalistrepros.formal-ssa.example.com
spec:
  group: formal-ssa.example.com
  scope: Cluster
  names:
    plural: ssalistrepros
[... 26 more lines]
```

A creates the populated object:

```
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=A -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: formal-ssa.example.com/v1
kind: SSAListRepro
metadata:
  name: repro
endpoints:
- name: db
  host: old
EOF
```

A now requests the valid empty list:

```
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=A -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: formal-ssa.example.com/v1
kind: SSAListRepro
metadata:
  name: repro
endpoints: []
EOF
```

The request fails validation because the proposed object lacks the required `endpoints` field. Repeating that exact request also fails. GET still returns the original item, original ownership and original resourceVersion.

As a control, apply the last manifest with a fresh name, e.g. `created-empty`. Creation succeeds and preserves `endpoints: []`.

For the CEL variant, use this root schema constraint **instead of** root `required: [endpoints]` when creating the CRD, and repeat with fresh objects:

```
# spec.versions[0].schema.openAPIV3Schema
type: object
x-kubernetes-validations:
- rule: has(self.endpoints)
# properties: ... unchanged ...
```

It has the same rejection/retry behavior.

Create the CRD without either root presence constraint, then repeat the same populated-to-empty transition. The real API-server/etcd test observes:

| Empty-list Apply by A | Persisted data | Persisted managedFields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Field absent | No managers remain |
| Second, identical | `endpoints: []` | No managers remain |
| Third, identical | `endpoints: []` | Synthetic `before-first-apply` Update owner claims `{"f:endpoints":{}}` |
| Fourth, identical | `endpoints: []` | Same ownership; storage no-op |

The first three requests each change resourceVersion. Only the first two change application data. This optional-field trace shows why a validator prevents retries from making progress: rejection preserves the old item claims that trigger the first transition.

For this known non-null granular list, Apply field-set extraction generates item/child claims but no direct list-presence claim, including for `[]`. Pruning removes the formerly owned list and has no new presence claim with which to restore the asserted empty list. The serialized FieldsV1 grammar itself can represent list presence; the synthetic Update owner above actually does so.

Reproduced with actual HTTP Apply against apiextensions-apiserver and etcd in [TestSSAEmptyAssociativeListPresence](https://github.com/sttts/kubernetes/blob/5fb5c47a82d97d753ad4879383adcff190e20564/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/test/integration/ssa_formal_test.go), covering optional, required and CEL schemas. Rejected requests are checked for unchanged data, FieldsV1 and resourceVersion; empty creation is checked under all three policies.

[PR #143805](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143805) contains those tests, [the full trace and source analysis](https://github.com/sttts/kubernetes/blob/5fb5c47a82d97d753ad4879383adcff190e20564/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/formal/docs/baseline-empty-list.md), and Lean counterexamples. The Lean results refute unrestricted immediate data idempotence and prove the presence-validation retry failure for every finite retry count in the stated model. Actual Go/API execution independently reproduces the concrete witness. The PR adds verification and characterization tests; it does not change production SSA behavior.

The inner SMD failure also reproduces on both pinned sides of [structured-merge-diff PR #336](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/structured-merge-diff/pull/336). It is a baseline bug, not caused by that unmerged proposal.

- #134902 also involves associative-list pruning and validation, but requires a non-SSA update and then omits the field. This reproduction uses only A's Apply requests and explicitly supplies an empty list.
- #131175 reports repeated no-op writes for a built-in ClusterRoleBinding. This report isolates loss of explicit list presence in a CRD and the resulting required/CEL retry failure.
- #104694 concerns the separate empty-granular-map-to-null transition.

Device allocation deferred to container start breaks PodResources API consumers that need devices at sandbox creation (e.g. Kata GPU cold-plug)

In Kubernetes 1.36 and 1.37, legacy device-plugin allocation (including nvidia.com/pgpu / nvidia.com/gpu) is deferred until container creation time.

In pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go (v1.37.0), AllocatePod is a no-op:

    func (m *ManagerImpl) AllocatePod(logger klog.Logger, pod *v1.Pod, _ lifecycle.Operation) error {
        // Device Manager does not support pod level resource allocation.
        // ...
    }

The device plugin’s Allocate RPC only fires when the container that requests the device is started — after RunPodSandbox.

Runtimes that query the kubelet PodResources API during sandbox preparation (to cold-plug devices into a VM) therefore see an empty device list:

    kata: pod cdi devices: []
    kata: no pod CDI devices requested.
    kata: raw VFIO cold-plug candidates: []
    kata: no pod devices to prepare for sandbox.

The VM boots without the GPU. When the GPU container later starts, the device arrives as an OCI spec device node using the iommufd cdev path (/dev/vfio/devices/vfioN). The hot-plug path cannot handle this path (it expects a classic /dev/vfio/<group> node), so StartContainer fails.

This reproduces deterministically with:
- Kubernetes 1.36 (when PodLevelResourceManagers is enabled) and 1.37 (unconditionally)
- Kata Containers 4.3.1
- NVIDIA GPU Operator sandbox device plugin (nvidia.com/pgpu)

Pods that use only container-level resources and do not hit the deferred path work. Any pod that relies on devices being allocated and visible via PodResources before sandbox creation fails.

Devices requested by a Pod should be allocated and visible via the PodResources API before RunPodSandbox, so that runtimes which must cold-plug devices (especially VFIO/GPU passthrough into a VM) can discover and attach them at sandbox creation time.

This was the previous behavior and is the contract documented by the NVIDIA GPU Operator for Kata (enable KubeletPodResourcesGet so the runtime can query allocated devices during sandbox prep).

Prerequisites:
- Kubernetes 1.36 or 1.37
- Feature gates enabled on the kubelet:
  - PodLevelResources=true
  - PodLevelResourceManagers=true
  - KubeletPodResourcesGet=true (required for Kata to query devices)
- Topology Manager policy set best-effort with topologyManagerScope: pod
- Static CPU Manager
- Static Memory Manager
- NVIDIA GPU Operator in sandbox/passthrough mode
- Kata Containers 4.3.1 runtime class

Failing case (pod-level CPU/memory + container-level GPU):

    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: gpu-coldplug-test3
      namespace: default
      labels:
        app: gpu-coldplug-test3
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: nvidia-6-18-56-615-71-09-standard
      restartPolicy: Never
      # REPRO: pod-level cpu/mem (PodLevelResourceManagers path) + container-level pgpu
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "2"
          memory: 2Gi
        limits:
          cpu: "2"
          memory: 2Gi
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: quay.io/k0sproject/pause:3.10.2-0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          resources:
            limits:
              nvidia.com/pgpu: "1"

Result: Pod stuck in StartError / Pending. Kata logs show empty CDI devices at sandbox prep. Device plugin Allocate fires only later at container creation. Hot-plug fails on the cdev path.

Working case (all resources at container level):

    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: gpu-coldplug-test4
      namespace: default
      labels:
        app: gpu-coldplug-test4
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: nvidia-6-18-56-615-71-09-standard
      restartPolicy: Never
      # FIX PROOF: no pod-level resources; cpu/mem on containers
      initContainers:
        - name: inject-init
          image: rig:tini
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          command: ["true"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 1m
              memory: 1Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 1m
              memory: 1Mi
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: quay.io/k0sproject/pause:3.10.2-0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: 2Gi
            limits:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: 2Gi
              nvidia.com/pgpu: "1"

Result: Pod reaches 1/1 Running. Kata receives the CDI device at sandbox prep and cold-plugs the GPU.

Minimal contrast:
- Same resources at pure container level → works (devices allocated early enough for cold-plug).
- Pod-level CPU/memory + container-level pgpu (with PodLevelResourceManagers and topologyManagerScope: pod) → fails on both 1.36 and 1.37.

Restore (or provide an explicit guarantee for) device allocation and PodResources visibility before sandbox creation for device-plugin resources. This allows VM runtimes that require cold-plug (Kata GPU/VFIO) to continue working without depending on a hot-plug path that does not support modern iommufd cdev device nodes.

Alternative acceptable approaches:
- A documented, supported way for a runtime to request that devices be allocated before RunPodSandbox.
- Make the device manager’s AllocatePod actually perform the allocation (or at least populate the PodResources API) for containers that request devices.

Impact

Any deployment using the NVIDIA sandbox device plugin (or any plugin that reports /dev/vfio/devices/vfio<N> DeviceSpecs) with Kata Containers on kubelet ≥ 1.36/1.37 is broken for GPU passthrough. This also affects other consumers of the PodResources API that expect devices to be present at sandbox creation time.

Related:
- Kata currently only cold-plugs at sandbox creation (get_pod_cdi_devices in sandbox prep).
- Hot-plug path does not handle iommufd cdev paths.
- I will also open a corresponding issue on the Kata side.

Can't distinguish APF throttling 429s from Eviction API (PDB) 429s based on client-go metrics

The kube-apiserver returns 429 for two very different reasons:
1. API Priority and Fairness rejected the request (queue full / timed out): the client, or the cluster as a whole, is sending too much traffic.
2. The Eviction API refused an eviction because it would violate a PodDisruptionBudget: a normal "not now" that says nothing about apiserver load.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cd72177dfedb5d894c3284771b29fde2d30bfabe/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L445

For cluster-autoscaler (and other clients that drain nodes) this means that we cannot understand what the problem is from the client-go metrics. To alert on "this component is overloading the apiserver", we need to count only (1), but `rest_client_requests_total{code="429"}` mixes in every PDB-blocked eviction retry.

Expected the response code 429 to be reserved for server-side throttling. Then a client can alert on "I'm overloading the apiserver".

portforward improperly closes local listener in response to server workload RST, breaking all subsequent connections

When the pod side resets one forwarded connection (TCP RST on the pod-local loopback hop), the container runtime reports an error for that connection and `kubectl port-forward` then exits with `error: lost connection to pod`.

The local listener terminates, so every other connection through the same port-forward, and every later one, fails with `connection refused`.

```
E1102 14:33:01.870223 portforward.go:424] "Unhandled Error" err="an error occurred forwarding 18445 -> 8443: error forwarding port 8443 to pod 3aa3d2dc..., uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace \"/var/run/netns/cni-...\": writeto tcp4 127.0.0.1:45472->127.0.0.1:8443: read tcp4 127.0.0.1:45472->127.0.0.1:8443: read: connection reset by peer"
error: lost connection to pod
```

The problem is that an error that should affect only one specific forwarded connection is improperly promoted to become a session-wide failure. When the server side sees the connection refused it writes it to that request's error stream and resets only that stream pair:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa8de068063335aee4a78589ee0d5c70b448e266/staging/src/k8s.io/cri-streaming/pkg/streaming/portforward/httpstream.go#L261-L262

But the client that receives it incorrectly turns it into a session-wide failure:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa8de068063335aee4a78589ee0d5c70b448e266/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go#L548-L550

`streamConn` is the one SPDY/websocket session shared by all forwarded connections. Closing it fires `CloseChan()`, `forward()` returns `ErrLostConnectionToPod`, and kubectl exits. That close was added deliberately in 4a35e6c5641 ("close streamConn and stop listening when an error occurs while port forwarding"), so this may be intended behaviour, but it makes one bad connection fatal for all of them.

This issue can also be indirectly triggered by a client-side RST such as a client timing out and abandoning a connection, explicit cancel of a browser page load, control-C on a client CLI, etc. In these cases the client action causes a _server_ RST, and the server RST is what breaks the port-forward.

I expected the error to be logged for the connection that failed, but the port-forward and its
other connections to keep working.

Existing connections other than the one with the error should continue to work. New connections should be able to be successfully established after the error.

_However_ the fix should avoid breaking the intent of the change that introduced it, #103526: If the pod that the port-forward targets exits, the port-forward client should exit, not hang indefinitely. #103526 closes the session on any error-stream message so that kubectl exits when the pod dies (kubectl/kubectl#686). The client can't tell that apart from a per-connection error such as a target RST, so it treats both as fatal.

This means a simplistic "fix" like

```
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go
index c5795264bf2..f8c8fe7af14 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go
@@ -546,8 +546,8 @@ func (pf *PortForwarder) handleConnection(conn net.Conn, port ForwardedPort) {
                runtime.HandleErrorWithLogger(pf.logger, errResult.err, "Error reading from error stream", "localPort", port.Local, "remotePort", port.Remote)
                pf.streamConn.Close()
        case len(errResult.message) > 0:
+               // Scoped to this connection: other forwarded connections must keep working.
                runtime.HandleErrorWithLogger(pf.logger, errors.New(string(errResult.message)), "An error occurred forwarding", "localPort", port.Local, "remotePort", port.Remote)
[... 3 more lines]
```

would _not_ be correct, as it'll subvert the intent of #103526

A self contained reproducer is attached: [repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34298309/repro.zip) - see `run.sh`. It requires a `go` toolchain, `kubectl` and `kind`.

View manual repro steps

Alternately, any workload that resets a connection reproduces it. E.g. a small Go server that answers 401 without reading the body and closes with `SO_LINGER 0`:

```
// Excerpt from server/main.go in repro.zip
//
conn, buf, _ := w.(http.Hijacker).Hijack()
buf.WriteString("HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n")
buf.Flush()
conn.(*tls.Conn).NetConn().(*net.TCPConn).SetLinger(0) // close sends RST
conn.Close()
```

1. Run it in a pod named `repro` on a `kind` cluster (listening on 8443).
2. `kubectl port-forward pod/repro 18445:8443`
3. Send sequential requests to `https://127.0.0.1:18445/`, e.g. 300 POSTs from a Go `http.Client` or a `curl --http1.1` loop.

Result: the first request or two succeed, then the error above, then `lost connection to pod`, then `connection refused` for the rest.

If the server is modified to close the socket normally (FIN) all 300 succeed.

I'll send a PR for this as I think this behaviour is clearly incorrect.

It was introduced by:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/103526

but this is over-broad; it's nonsensical to exit when a connection error occurs due to an RST from the port-forward target in the pod (rather than the kubelet or kube runtime); such errors are common, normal and can be transient.

This quite likely the cause of reports such as:

* #111825 (psql `\c` closes the forward with the same `connection reset by peer` error)
* #107203
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/78446
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74551

Reproduced with containerd 2.0.3 (`kindest/node:v1.32.3`). The runtime only needs to report an error for one connection so CRI-O probably behaves the same but this is unverified.

I first encountered this issue years ago when fighting reliability problems with port-forwarding Grafana, Loki's `logcli`, etc. I always suspected the port-forward broke due to a _client side_ connection interruption or reset. So I never traced it down until now.

LLM assistance was used to find this issue and draft an initial report, which I then checked, edited, clarified and corrected.

e2e tests for consistency between allocation manager and CPU manager on in-place resize of exclusive CPUs

e2e_node tests for the scenarios that motivated #143400, added after both #140629 and #143400 are merged.

In #140629 the CPU manager committed a resize inside its admit handler, before the remaining containers and admit handlers were evaluated ([review](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140629#pullrequestreview-5520566858)). When the resize was then rejected, the CPU manager state and the allocation manager state could diverge, and CPUs could leak until the pod was deleted. #143400 makes resize admission a transaction: the CPU manager prepares the resize and commits it only after the allocation is persisted.

Each scenario uses a Guaranteed pod with exclusive CPUs and the static CPU manager policy.

1. **Rejected after the CPU manager allocated CPUs**: the resize changes CPU and memory. The CPU manager can allocate the new CPUs, but a later step rejects the resize, e.g. the memory manager cannot align the memory with the NUMA node. Expected: the resize is not admitted and everything stays as before it; the containers keep their original cpusets, and the CPUs the resize would have taken stay in the shared pool.
2. **Partially admitted pod**: a pod with two containers; the CPU manager can allocate the new CPUs for the first container but not for the second, e.g. there are not enough free CPUs on the NUMA node. Expected: the resize is not admitted; the first container keeps its original cpuset, not the one prepared for it during admission.
3. **No leaked CPUs**: after a rejected resize, a new pod can get all the CPUs that were free before the resize.
4. **Resize reverted**: the spec goes back to the original values after a rejected resize. Nothing from the rejected attempt remains in the CPU manager state.
5. **Kubelet restart after a rejected resize**: the pod is admitted again, keeps its original cpuset, and no CPUs are lost.
6. **Kubelet restart after an admitted resize**: the pod keeps the resized cpuset.

A restart between persisting the allocation and the CPU manager commit cannot be hit reliably in e2e; it stays covered by unit tests.

CPUmanager: replace `removeStaleState` with explicit release of CPUs

Follow-up to #143400, as agreed in [this review](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143400#pullrequestreview-5710091171): use the admission transaction added by #143400 to remove `removeStaleState` from the CPU manager and make the reconcile loop leaner.

- #143202, [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143202#issuecomment-6299274528): the reconcile loop has two responsibilities, removing stale state and fixing the default cpuset of containers without exclusive CPUs; moving the first one close to admission is beneficial.
- #143202, [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143202#issuecomment-6366887250): an explicit undo on failed admission removes a good portion of the reconcile loop and releases CPUs earlier (better pod density).
- #143202, [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143202#issuecomment-6326514624): there is no explicit hook to release CPUs today.
- #143202, [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/143202#issuecomment-6297932442): the plan from #142430, i.e. partitions first, then actuation in `syncPod` and removal of the reconcile loop.
- #140629, [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140629#discussion_r4306197603): do not add more logic to the reconcile loop; work gradually towards eliminating it.
- #140629, [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140629#discussion_r4273387867): pod addition tolerates writing state during admission only because `removeStaleState` reclaims the CPUs of rejected pods.

- `removeStaleState` is the only path that releases CPUs. It runs before every `Allocate`, `AllocatePod`, `GetTopologyHints` and `GetPodTopologyHints`, and on every reconcile pass ([cpu_manager.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c94a6cca22588f5bcc9c0ed2e56b96a762d2082f/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_manager.go#L432-L499)).
- `Manager.RemoveContainer` has no external callers; `PostStopContainer` only notifies the topology manager.
- It cleans up three kinds of stale state:
  1. pods rejected at admission after the CPU manager allocated CPUs for them,
  2. terminated or deleted pods,
  3. pods that disappeared while the kubelet was down.
- Rejected resizes no longer leave stale state since #143400.

1. Run pod addition through the admission transaction: on `CompleteAdmit(AdmitFailure)` the CPU manager releases the CPUs it allocated for the pod.
2. Release CPUs explicitly when a pod terminates. The kubelet hook is to be decided; CPUs of a restarting container must be kept.
3. Clean up once after kubelet restart, when pod sources are ready.
4. Remove `removeStaleState` from the allocation and hint paths and from `reconcileState`.

Steps 1–3 are independent; step 4 needs all of them. The memory manager uses the same pattern; whether it is in scope is open.

Fixing the default cpuset of containers without exclusive CPUs and removing the reconcile loop entirely; this needs #142430.

`NewSourceURL` in `pkg/kubelet/config/http.go` starts a polling goroutine that can never be stopped:

```

It also sends on the unbuffered `updates` channel in three places in `extractFromURL` (empty data, single pod, pod list) with plain `s.updates <- ...` sends. The URL source stops polling when the kubelet context is canceled, and no send on `updates` can block after that.

A goleak check in `pkg/kubelet/config` shows the polling goroutine still running after the test:

Kubelet re-runs terminated ephemeral containers when their runtime container is removed

The kubelet decides whether to start an ephemeral container only by checking whether the runtime still has a container with that name ([`computePodActions`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d0d1a17193d42dab5e893d21266bc5f8de16735f/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1412-L1419)):

```
// Ephemeral Containers are never restarted
if podStatus.FindContainerStatusByName(c.Name) == nil {
	changes.EphemeralContainersToStart = append(changes.EphemeralContainersToStart, i)
}
```

If the exited container is removed from the runtime, the next pod sync starts the ephemeral container again and re-runs its command. Each removal leads to one more run.

**The re-run container doesn't show up in the pod status while it runs.** The API rejects the kubelet's status update (`status.ephemeralContainerStatuses[0].state: Forbidden: may not be transitioned to non-terminated state`). So the status keeps reporting the original run as `Terminated`, with its old `containerID` and `restartCount: 0`, while a new container is running in the pod. The status only catches up once the re-run exits. A re-run that never exits (e.g. a shell or a long-running command) stays invisible for the life of the pod, and nothing in the API shows that it's running.

Regular containers that shouldn't restart (`restartPolicy: Never`, or `OnFailure` after exit 0) have the same problem if the pod is still running. [`ShouldContainerBeRestarted`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d0d1a17193d42dab5e893d21266bc5f8de16735f/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L95-L101) returns true when no runtime container exists, and has a comment noting this also happens if all historical containers were GC'd. Non-restartable init containers are not affected: once a regular container has started, the kubelet treats the pod as initialized.

With the default kubelet GC settings, container GC (periodic, and disk-pressure reclaim) always keeps the newest dead instance of each container in a running pod, so GC alone doesn't trigger this. It can happen when:

- the kubelet runs with non-default `--maximum-dead-containers` (≥ 0) or `--maximum-dead-containers-per-container=0`;
- exited containers are removed outside the kubelet (e.g. `crictl rm`, cleanup scripts);
- the runtime loses its container state (e.g. a runtime configured to wipe containers after a reboot).

Verified on v1.37.2 (kind, containerd 2.3.1).

```
$ kubectl run target --image=registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
$ kubectl debug target --image=busybox --container=debugger -- sh -c 'echo ran; sleep 30'

# On the node, once the ephemeral container has exited:
$ crictl rm $(crictl ps -aq --name debugger)

# Wait for the next pod sync (~1 min), or a few seconds later force one:
$ kubectl label pod target resync=1

$ crictl ps -a --name debugger   # the new container is Running
[... 2 more lines]

Strategic merge patch with `"$deleteFromPrimitiveList/<field>": null` deletes the whole field instead of no element

A strategic merge patch whose `$deleteFromPrimitiveList/<field>` directive is `null` returns 200 and
deletes `<field>` entirely. `{"metadata":{"$deleteFromPrimitiveList/finalizers":null}}` removes every
finalizer, and the same directive on `labels` or `data` removes all labels or the whole `data` map.
A list with no matching value, an empty list and a plain string all leave the field alone.

The [strategic merge patch description](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/contributors/devel/sig-api-machinery/strategic-merge-patch.md#deletefromprimitivelist-directive)
says: "`deleteFromPrimitiveList` directive indicates that the elements in this list should be
deleted from the original primitive list." A `null` value lists no element.

A Go client that builds the patch from a nil `[]string` sends `null`, and the object loses all its
finalizers. On an object that is being deleted, that also deletes the object.

`metadata.finalizers` stays unchanged, as with `[]`, or the patch fails with 400. The same for
`labels` and `data`.

```
kubectl create -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cm-d26
  labels: {a: "1", b: "2"}
  finalizers: ["example.com/f", "example.com/g"]
data: {k: v}
EOF

[... 10 more lines]
```

Output (v1.37.2):

```
configmap/cm-d26 created
["example.com/f","example.com/g"]
["example.com/f","example.com/g"]
["example.com/f","example.com/g"]

labels= data=
```

The first three patches change nothing. The fourth removes both finalizers (empty line), and the
fifth removes all labels and `data`. All five return 200.

**Potential cause.** In `mergeMap`, the `patchV == nil` branch deletes the original field before
`isDeleteList` is checked
([`patch.go#L1349-L1373`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/386245def96934751c6fe8014aa9a9a0b60f7ab8/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/strategicpatch/patch.go#L1349-L1373)).

**Suggested fix.** Skip that deletion when `isDeleteList` is set, or return
`mergepatch.ErrBadPatchFormatForPrimitiveList` for a directive value that is not a list.

Not a regression: v1.34.1 behaves the same.

Server-side apply that removes a manager's last finalizer also removes the `foregroundDeletion` or `orphan` finalizer, and the object is deleted at once

A controller adds its finalizer with server-side apply and later removes it by applying its
configuration without the finalizer. If the object is being deleted with
`propagationPolicy=Foreground` or `Orphan`, the API server has added `foregroundDeletion` or
`orphan` to `metadata.finalizers`, and no field manager owns that entry.

The controller's apply removes the whole list, including `foregroundDeletion`/`orphan`. The object
has a `deletionTimestamp` and no finalizers left, so it is deleted in the same request:

- With `Foreground`, the owner is gone while a dependent with `blockOwnerDeletion: true` still
  exists.
- With `Orphan`, if the garbage collector has not processed `orphan` yet, it later deletes the
  dependents the user asked to keep.

This happens only when the apply drops the applier's last finalizer. If another manager still owns
a finalizer, or if the finalizer is removed with a JSON patch, `foregroundDeletion`/`orphan` stays.

[Server-Side Apply, Merge strategy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/server-side-apply/#merge-strategy):
"If the set of items present in the applied config is not a superset of the items applied by the
same user last time, each missing item not managed by any other appliers is removed."
`my-controller` never applied `foregroundDeletion`. Removing a controller's finalizer with
server-side apply during a foreground deletion is the pattern recommended in #111643.

The apply removes only `example.com/cleanup`. `foregroundDeletion` stays, and the garbage collector
deletes `parent` once `child` is gone, as it does when the finalizer is removed with a JSON patch.

Any cluster with the garbage collector running (for example `kind create cluster`):

```
cat <<EOF > parent.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: parent
  finalizers: ["example.com/cleanup"]
data: {k: v}
EOF
cat <<EOF > parent-cleanup-done.yaml
apiVersion: v1
[... 27 more lines]
```

Output (v1.37.2):

```
configmap/parent serverside-applied
configmap/child created
configmap "parent" deleted from default namespace
NAME     DELETING               FINALIZERS
parent   2026-10-29T15:54:00Z   [example.com/cleanup foregroundDeletion]
child    2026-10-29T15:54:00Z   [example.com/hold]
Warning: Detected changes to resource parent which is currently being deleted.
configmap/parent serverside-applied
NAME    DELETING               FINALIZERS
child   2026-10-29T15:54:00Z   [example.com/hold]
[... 1 more lines]
```

`parent` is gone while `child` still blocks it. With the last apply replaced by
`kubectl patch configmap parent --type=json -p '[{"op":"test","path":"/metadata/finalizers/0","value":"example.com/cleanup"},{"op":"remove","path":"/metadata/finalizers/0"}]'`,
`parent` stays with `[foregroundDeletion]`.

**Potential cause.** In structured-merge-diff's `Updater.prune`, `EnsureNamedFieldsAreMembers` puts
the field `metadata.finalizers` itself into the applier's last applied set
([`merge/update.go#L270`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/structured-merge-diff/blob/560aaa513ea735bf59e6011feecd5388e2dfeae9/merge/update.go#L270)).
When the applier drops its last item, `addBackDanglingItems` removes that field as a whole, with the
unowned item in it
([`merge/update.go#L342-L365`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/structured-merge-diff/blob/560aaa513ea735bf59e6011feecd5388e2dfeae9/merge/update.go#L342-L365)).
The delete handler adds the GC finalizer without recording a field manager, so no manager keeps it.

**Suggested fix.** Remove a list or map field as a whole only when no item outside the applier's
last applied set is left in it.
